Elon Musk and The Rise of Cult Capitalism
Every billionaire is a policy failure. The first trillionaire is also a market failure.
Adam Bonica
Jun 19, 2026
If every billionaire is a policy failure, what then is a trillionaire? The world’s first is more than an unprecedented policy failure. It is also an unprecedented market failure.

At $1.32 trillion, Elon Musk’s net worth is no longer a measure of corporate earnings; it is an exercise in cult capitalism. His wealth is underwritten entirely by collective faith in his power to deliver a future that has not yet arrived. The market is not tracking traditional value—it is pricing belief. Musk’s fortune is the world's first trillion-dollar pitch deck.

Musk owns large stakes in Tesla and SpaceX, the market prices them, the total is his fortune. But look at what the market is appraising. SpaceX went public this month at a valuation near $1.77 trillion, the largest IPO in history. In 2025 it lost $4.9 billion, and the losses are accelerating: $4.28 billion in the first quarter of 2026 alone, against an accumulated deficit of $41.3 billion. Tesla, for its part, earned $3.8 billion last year, a profit but an ordinary one. Put the two together and the foundation of the largest personal fortune in human history ran a combined net loss in 2025.

To be up front, these are not worthless companies. But whether they’re worth something is the wrong question. In this respect they are no different from the carmakers, tech firms, and defense contractors they compete with. The real question is the gap: the trillions of dollars of value sitting above anything earnings or market conditions can explain, and what fills it. Are Musk’s companies truly special?

I built a chart to put this in perspective. It plots fortunes at one pixel per thousand dollars, and Musk’s bar runs on for an incomprehensibly long time. It is an absurd spectacle and a tragic one: a Mississippi-sized river of pixels and forgone futures, its banks strewn with everything our society could have built instead. The schools, the cures, the fed children, the economic security of millions. All of it routed into the net worth of one man.

It is one of the oldest buildings left standing in the entire Mississippi Valley, and it survived the very fire that burned nearly everything else in New Orleans to the ground. 🏚️⚜️

They call it Madame John's Legacy, a raised Creole residence on Dumaine Street in the French Quarter. Most visitors walk right past it, drawn to the grander iron laced mansions nearby. But this humble wooden house is a rare and precious survivor, a window into the French colonial world that almost nothing else in the Quarter can offer.

Here is the twist that surprises people. 🔥

The French Quarter we picture, with its Spanish courtyards and cast iron galleries, is not actually French. It is largely Spanish, rebuilt after two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed the original French colonial town. Almost every trace of early French New Orleans went up in flames. But Madame John's Legacy, rebuilt in 1788 in the old French West Indian style right after the first fire, endured, and it shows us what the lost city truly looked like.

Its design is a lesson in survival, raised high on a brick ground floor to escape the floods, wrapped in a shaded gallery to breathe in the heat, built of cypress that resists rot and time. This was architecture shaped by the land itself, by water and sun and hard experience.

The name comes from a nineteenth century short story, not a real Madame John, but the house is real enough, and it has watched over Dumaine Street for well over two centuries. In a city that has lost so much to fire and flood and the wrecking ball, this quiet old house is a miracle of endurance. Some things in Louisiana simply refuse to disappear. 

From Louisiana Unbound

xAI Is Buying 418 Mississippi Homes to Kill a Lawsuit Before It Forms

A subsidiary of Elon Musk's xAI is offering to purchase 418 homes in a Southaven, Mississippi neighborhood, according to reports from The Guardian and the Mississippi Free Press. The condition of sale: residents must not join an existing lawsuit targeting the company's adjacent data center and power plant. A realtor going door-to-door reportedly disclosed the scope of the plan, with 18 homeowners already committed to selling.

The offer's structure makes its purpose legible without much interpretation. xAI needs the extinguishment of a plaintiff class, not the land itself. Homeowners who accept get an undisclosed price and waive their legal standing. Renters — who have nothing xAI needs to acquire — receive no offer. They receive 60 days' notice after their landlords agree to sell, then the door.

The displacement of renters is the collateral output of the mechanism, not its target. Once landlords accept, renters move. That's structurally inevitable, not incidental. What's being acquired isn't just property — it's the community's capacity to consolidate into a plaintiff class before the lawsuit gains mass.

This extends a pattern already visible in xAI's litigation history. Earlier moves involved procedural pressure on existing plaintiffs — deepfake harm claimants, a lawsuit against Minnesota AG Keith Ellison to block a nudification law. The Southaven approach is the same logic applied one step upstream: rather than contesting plaintiffs who already exist, remove the standing before the class forms. The instrument is economic acquisition rather than motion practice, but the objective is identical.

The buyout terms remain undisclosed. That opacity is unremarkable for private transactions. What is on the record is the condition itself, and the condition is the substance of what's happening here. Infrastructure expansion generating neighborhood externalities — noise, emissions, power-plant operations — and the operational response being residential acquisition with liability waivers attached. Both the builder credit and this entry sit on the same ledger, and neither cancels the other.

text:
I’m Inspired

For the last 12 years, I’ve been playing soccer.

I’ve played in various leagues across the metro area. For a long time, it was mostly indoor “wall soccer.” But for the last 6 years, I’ve only played in 9v9 and 11v11 full field matches. I’ve found that the level of play, when the rules are applied, like outs, offsides, and other various factors, makes the game much more challenging and beautiful. For the most part, I’ve found myself always trying to find the best leagues to play in with the most competitive teams, but it’s still just weekday soccer, and I feel I’ve found that. I feel I’ve been playing with some of the better amateur players Colorado has to offer without the full commitment. Lots of the players in the league play in the CPL and even UPSL. One of the teams is actually a UPSL team and another a CPL team. So, for this, I’m grateful. Grateful I’ve been able to play at a high level.

Tonight, I had a match at Foothills Sports Arena. We played an older squad, but an experienced squad. We were winning 2 to 1, but we were being played well. Lots of challenges on the ball, and lots of dangerous plays coming our way from the opposition.

It was the 45th minute in a 60 minute match.

I got a long ball from my center back. I was roughly between the half field and the 18 yard line on the left wing. This ball was perfect, on pace and in the air. I chested the ball down, and I looked up at the goalie and saw he was slightly out of place. I let the ball bounce, and I wound up and just let it rip. I hit a perfect volley from distance, and it was a bullet. This ball sailed up and immediately had a strong dip. I hit the far post of the goal, all side net in the upper corner. There was no chance the goalie was going to get this ball. It was just a banger.

To be honest, there’s no high like it. Hitting a goal like that, it’s as if time slowed down. You’re in the zone, you see the perfect opportunity, and you just execute. It’s as if everything just lined up for that moment to happen. It’s an unreal joy and excitement.

This euphoria, this flow state, this is something I don’t actually believe everyone gets to experience. And this just truly makes me thankful. It makes me thankful because playing sports, or having a hobby and achieving something you’ve been working at, is just amazing. It gives me so much to be thankful for. Thankful I can still move, thankful I can still compete. But also thankful for just life, that the opportunity is there. Thankful for my kids, my wife, my family, and everything in between. I know it’s just the high talking from the goal, but truly, life is full of surprises, good and bad. And I’m just grateful.

Get out there, try something new, get a hobby. Of course, don’t go crazy. Stay within your limits. But test the boundaries, see how far you can make it.

text:
Cadillac had a rule against selling cars to Black people, and its service bays kept filling up with Black people's Cadillacs. The owners were handing a white stranger the full price of a car plus several hundred dollars to walk in, sign his own name, and bring the keys back out to the sidewalk.

When Nicholas Dreystadt took it to the General Motors board in 1932, his argument was not that the rule was wrong, it was that somebody outside the building was collecting a fee the building had created. Read the argument that actually moved that room, not the one we prefer to remember.

There were Cadillac showrooms in New Orleans in the 1950s and 1960s that almost never had a Black person on the floor. When one did come through the door, the odds were that they had come to clean the place.

Lillian Gadison Brown came in to buy a Cadillac.

Some of the salesmen laughed at her where she stood. Others were more constructive about it and walked her back out toward the used lot, where she was welcome to look over some beaten Chevrolets.

She kept going. Not the same dealership every time, and not once.

That kind of no is never about the money, and every person on the floor knows it. The man saying it has already looked her over, made his estimate, and decided to send her out back to somebody else's worn-out car with no interest at all in what she had in her purse.

The woman he sent out back was a Black French Creole from New Iberia, living with her husband and their six children in the Lower Ninth Ward, which was Black for the simple reason that most of the rest of the city would not have them. In the language of Black New Orleans, the Browns were a professional family.

Her husband Daniel Brown had come home from the war with the Army Medical Corps behind him, Italy and North Africa, and he wanted to be a doctor. Tulane would not admit a Black student to any part of the university until 1963, and the medical school at Louisiana State did not take one until 1952, and only because a court made it.

There was nowhere in his own state to put him.

So he went back to Xavier, where he had done his pre-med before the war, and he spent the rest of his life turning other people's children into doctors and pharmacists instead. The Browns had a name for what had been done to them, and they used it often enough that their son could still repeat it in his sixties, that they were victims of status discrepancy.

Naming it was not the same as hiding behind it. When their son Warren accused a white priest at his high school of failing him out of racism, his father sat him down with the geometry and made him work every problem in front of him.

The boy could not do a single one. His father told him the priest might well be a racist, and that it would not matter one bit until he could do the work.

Then he walked out of the room.

That is the house the Cadillac question came out of, and it came out of that house because of the buses. In New Orleans in the 1950s, if you did not have a car you rode the bus, and if you rode the bus you sat behind the sign.

Lillian Gadison Brown would walk before she did that, or telephone one of the colored cab companies, or catch a ride off somebody in the Ninth Ward with a truck. Her husband did not have that option every day, and the children saw what it cost him.

Daniel Brown was a talker. He would be going the whole way to the stop, cheerful, one or two of the six with him, and then he would put his foot on the step of a New Orleans city bus and something in him would shut off.

He went silent. Not quiet, silent, and cold with it, and he stayed that way the entire ride while his children sat next to him and watched a man they knew disappear into himself.

Then the bus reached their stop and they climbed down onto the sidewalk, and their father came back. He did that for years, in front of his children, every time he had to board one.

The solution to it was obvious and it was Lillian Gadison Brown who kept putting it on the table. She would start at dinner, aimed at her husband, always the same argument, that a car of their own would put an end to the entire business, and some nights it ran for hours.

Their son put in his own suggestion, still small, which was that they buy a Chevrolet and go see the country, because that was what the lady sang in the television commercials. What they finally got was a Rambler.

It was smaller than the winged Bel Air the boy had his heart set on, and it was not a Cadillac, and none of that turned out to matter at all. What mattered was that the six of them could get in it and go where they were going without anybody telling them where to sit, and that their mother and father, for the length of the drive, were nobody's second-class anything.

The Rambler solved the bus. It did not open the showroom door, and she would spend the next decade working her way around that door instead.

The reason it was shut was written down nowhere, and it was already thirty years old before she ever reached for the handle.

Through the 1920s and into the 1930s, Cadillac was chasing what the company itself called the prestige market, and one of the ways it protected that market was by refusing to sell to Black people. No memo carried the rule, and none needed to, because the dealers understood it and it held.

The trouble was that the service bays kept filling up with cars the company had not sold.

The man walking through those bays was Nicholas Dreystadt, who ran Cadillac's service operation across the entire country, city after city, year after year. He kept finding big new Cadillacs up on the lifts for routine work with Black owners sitting out front waiting on them, and the arithmetic would not close.

He asked, and the answer was that the customers had solved the problem years before anybody in Detroit noticed there was one. You found a white man who would do it, you paid him several hundred dollars on top of the full price of the car, and you sent him through the door to sign his name in the place where yours would not be accepted.

The white man came out with the keys and handed them over on the sidewalk. The paperwork left that building carrying his name.

Look at what that asks of a person. You are handing a stranger the entire price of an automobile plus a fee, on the strength of nothing but his word, at a moment in American history when a Black man's word against a white man's was not a contest that went anywhere.

Black buyers were doing it in Chicago and Detroit and New York and New Orleans, and doing it often enough that one service manager kept running into the evidence in every city he visited.

What that service manager found got written down years later by Peter Drucker, who was brought inside General Motors in 1943 to study how the company was put together and who knew Dreystadt personally. A Cadillac was the one success symbol an affluent Black American could actually go out and purchase, because the good neighborhoods were closed, the resorts were closed, and the clubs were closed.

Money could not buy a house on the right street. It could buy a car, and a car could be parked on any street in America.

None of which mattered to anybody in Detroit until Cadillac started dying. By 1933 sales had fallen roughly eighty-four percent from where they stood in 1928, and General Motors called its executive committee together to decide what to do with the division.

The options were to shut it down outright or keep the nameplate on a shelf and wait for better years, and the weight in that room, Alfred Sloan included, was toward letting it go.

Nicholas Dreystadt was not in that room. He was a middle manager out of the service organization, a German who had come over in 1912 at twenty-two off the Mercedes racing team, and nobody on that committee had any particular reason to know his name.

One historian measured what he did next this way, that it was roughly a monsignor knocking on the door of the Sistine Chapel to offer the cardinals a suggestion while they were busy electing a pope. He knocked, and he asked for ten minutes.

No minute book records what happened inside. Everything anyone knows about that meeting comes from Drucker, who had it from Dreystadt himself and wrote it down decades later.

They let him in, and he stood in front of the men who ran the largest industrial company on earth and told them about the Black doctors and boxers and entertainers whose cars he had been servicing for years. He told them about the white men standing in at the counter, and about the several hundred dollars a car those middlemen were collecting for it.

Then he asked why that money was going to them instead of to General Motors. That is the argument that ended the policy.

Not that the rule was unjust, and not that the customers had been humiliated, and not that a company selling to a man's proxy while refusing the man himself had made itself ridiculous. The argument that moved that room was that somebody outside the building was collecting a fee the building had created.

They gave him eighteen months, in 1932 by most accounts and a year later by some. Sales rose about seventy percent in 1934, the division broke even, and that June he was made general manager of Cadillac.

What actually changed there was narrower than the story usually allows. Cadillac stopped telling its dealers to turn Black customers away, and there is little sign it then went looking for Black customers.

Researchers went back through the Pittsburgh Courier, the Afro-American and the Chicago Defender across that entire decade and found no Cadillac advertising for new cars in any of them. Another writer on this history says dealers did buy space in those papers eventually, and the two accounts have never been squared.

What did turn up in those pages were used Cadillacs in the classifieds, placed there by whoever happened to be selling one.

The company that had just been talked into taking Black money was in no hurry to ask for more of it in print. Cadillac's own advertising stayed entirely white into the 1970s, and a former Cadillac spokesman, asked about that stretch in 1995, said it was the history and it was the way they were.

Detroit could change a policy on paper. It could not reach into every showroom in the country and change the man standing on the floor.

Which is how a salesman in New Orleans was still laughing at Lillian Gadison Brown thirty years after Detroit had stopped telling him to.

So she built a method instead. She worked the white men she already had access to, the ones she answered to, and she was patient about it, waiting until a man started talking about buying new and then offering to take the old one off his hands at a price he could live with.

It worked more than once. Over the years the Browns owned a Chevrolet Impala and several Cadillacs, including one snazzy coupe, and every last one of them came to her the long way around.

In 1965 she got the one she wanted. She crossed the parish line out to Metairie and bought it off a rich white man out there at what she judged to be a good price, a Coupe DeVille, midnight blue, cream white top, white leather inside, whitewall tires.

Thirty-three years after Nicholas Dreystadt stood up in that boardroom, she had her Cadillac the way Black buyers had been getting them all along, which was through a white man's hands.

And she saw to it that car was cleaned every week of its life. She handed out the assignments and she supervised, and the standing instruction to her children was clean soft cloths and do not scratch my car.

Then she would back it down the driveway and drive out to the Schwegmann's in east New Orleans, and her son wrote years later that she went to make groceries carrying herself like a woman on her way to a ball.

The country has had an explanation ready for cars like that one for ninety years. Black folks and their Cadillacs, chrome bought with money nobody had.

A big car was equipment. If you were Black and driving any distance in this country, no motel was obliged to rent you a room and no restaurant was obliged to seat you, so the car had to do both jobs.

Families packed the food for the whole trip and blankets for the children, and carried spare fuel and a spare belt, because a breakdown in the wrong county at the wrong hour was not an inconvenience. Gretchen Sorin, who spent years on the history of Black driving, found that the car Black families most often bought was not the Cadillac at all.

It was the cheaper Buick, chosen because it was reliable and because the seats were wide enough to sleep on. Sorin also found that Black Americans own Cadillacs at the same rate white Americans do, three percent against three percent.

The car was never the point. What the car did was the point, and the whole movement ran on it.

Montgomery held its bus boycott together for a year on private cars, Black people with vehicles hauling Black people without them. In New Orleans the Brown children ran a smaller version nobody named, walking and sharing rides and quietly staying off the city buses, which is the exact thing their father had told them to keep out of.

Forty years on, standing over the water in the Lower Ninth Ward after Katrina, Warren Brown followed that thought all the way down. The middle-income Black families had moved out of the ward once the law let them and had taken their cars with them, and he wondered how many people drowned for want of a neighbor with a ride.

His mother's own Cadillac never lasted long enough to see any of it. The Coupe DeVille ended when a teenage driver put it into the brick wall of a church.

Lillian Gadison Brown did not go get another one. She bought a Chevrolet Celebrity and a Chevrolet Cavalier instead, and when her son asked her about it she told him she was not going through shopping a Cadillac dealer again, and that the Chevrolet people were nicer.

Lillian Gadison Brown died in February 1995 at seventy-one, still enrolled part time, still a few credits short of the degree she had been chipping at for years. The car in her name at the end was a Ford Taurus.

They buried her out of Xavier, where she had worked for forty years and where all six of her children took their degrees, with Norman Francis, the president, in the church. Four decades inside the school that sends more Black students into medical school than any other in America, and her husband had been turned away from two of them.

Her family carried her to the cemetery in a line of Cadillacs. Fleetwoods and DeVille Concours sedans, an Eldorado somewhere in it, and one of her sons out in the procession driving that week's press car, a 1995 Seville.

She rode in more Cadillacs on the day of her funeral than anyone in her city ever sold her.

Ten months after they put her in the ground, Cadillac brought automotive journalists to Detroit to introduce a diversity marketing program, the first at General Motors and the model the rest of the company would copy. On the way out, the company handed everybody a magazine article about its own history.

The article was called The Man Who Saved the Cadillac. It had run in American Heritage that November, and it told the whole thing, the ten minutes and the front men and the boardroom.

Warren Brown stood in that room holding it, ten months after burying his mother.

On Christmas Eve he printed her name in the Washington Post.

Because the record had kept Dreystadt whole. It kept the Swabian accent and the tweed jackets burned through by his own pipe and the spare dress shoes his secretary held back for the mornings he came in wearing two that did not match, and it has kept them for ninety years and counting.

Of the people who built the market he noticed, it kept nothing at all. Drucker set them down as black entertainers, black boxers, black doctors, black realtors, and that is as close to a name as any of them ever got.

Somebody in there was the first to think of it. Somebody worked out the fee and found a white man who would take it and then stood on a sidewalk in 1931 with empty hands, waiting on a stranger to come back out with the keys to a car already paid for.

No archive is holding those names, because nobody wrote them down while it was happening. A kitchen might be.

Ask the oldest person you have left which one in the family had to buy something sideways, through a white man, and what the extra money cost the house that year.

Lillian Gadison Brown is in the record for exactly one reason, which is that one of her six children grew up to write about cars for a living.

And the Cadillac she is remembered for is the one nobody in her city would sell her.

text:
Honest American answer: yes, there were alternatives. Historians still argue over whether any of them would have ended the war sooner with fewer deaths. Here's what the record shows for each option:

🤝 Diplomacy
The US was reading Japan's secret cables. Tokyo was asking the USSR to help negotiate, but it would not accept unconditional surrender. The hardliners wanted to keep the Emperor and also to avoid an occupation. Secretary of War Stimson urged Truman to say up front that the Emperor could stay. That wasn't offered until after the bombs, and the US let him stay anyway. This is the strongest "what if."
https://t.co/IHi6IO8As7

🛢 Blockade
Japan was already being starved and burned out. The US Strategic Bombing Survey (1946) concluded Japan probably would have surrendered by Nov–Dec 1945 with no bombs, no Soviet entry, and no invasion. Caveats: that assumed the firebombing of cities would continue, and later historians said the Survey claimed more than its evidence could support.
https://t.co/go1RQO5fht

⚔️ Invasion
It was planned for Nov 1, 1945, on Kyushu. US codebreakers saw Japan massing far more troops there than planners had expected. It would almost certainly have been the deadliest option for both sides.
https://t.co/3RHHn8nRzg

⏳ Waiting
Hiroshima, the Soviet declaration of war, and Nagasaki all came within about 3 days. After all three, Japan's war council was still split 3–3 on surrendering. The Emperor had to break the tie himself.
https://t.co/U7AU95D33A

Army officers then tried a coup to stop the surrender broadcast.
https://t.co/m4A007VDTs

Many historians now argue the Soviet entry shook Tokyo as much as the bombs did.
https://t.co/SYkFjAV92d

Bottom line: a mix of guaranteeing the Emperor, Soviet entry, and blockade might have worked without the bombs, but nobody can prove it, since Japan's leaders were still deadlocked after both bombs. Americans honestly disagree on this one.

text:
Arthur Shawcross is a full-blown psychopath, and it shows in the first minute. He jokes that he's not scared of hell because at least he won't be lonely there. He killed two children, served less than 15 years and walked out on parole. Within 2 years, 11 more women were dead along the Genesee River. Now he's serving 25 life terms, laughing for the camera, while doctors find a dent in his skull and a cyst in his brain they say explains everything.

In the video below, the man the press called the Genesee River Killer sits down like he's at a barbecue.

Ask him about the words "serial killer" and he offers to read you a poem he wrote about it. He talks about Psycho. Says he didn't really enjoy it. Zero guilt. Zero discomfort. Just a guy shooting the breeze.

Then the doctors come in.

A sledgehammer to the head as a kid. A discus to the skull. The neurologist parts his hair and finds the dent. Then a scar on the other side.

The MRI shows a white spot in the part of the brain that controls impulses. A cyst in the right temporal lobe, bigger than it should be. An EEG spiking right in the same place.

Then the test that no one can argue with. The doctor strokes the bottom of his right foot. His big toe moves up. Just a few millimeters. That tiny movement means a major pathway in his brain is damaged. "There could be no controversy over that."

Shawcross listens to all of it and says something chilling. Sometimes he wonders if somebody tampered with him.

His story was full of lies too. He told psychiatrists he killed and ate people in Vietnam. Army records showed he never saw combat.

He was caught in January 1990 by a police helicopter. It spotted him parked on a bridge, right above the body of one of his victims.

At trial, his defense said brain damage and a brutal childhood made him a killer. The jury didn't buy it. 25 years for each of the 10 murders he was tried for. 250 years total.

From his cell, he sold his own paintings to collectors. He died in prison in 2008, at 63.

The doctor's conclusion is the scariest part. Most abused kids never hurt anyone. Most people with brain damage never kill. Put both in one person, and you get Arthur Shawcross.

Some lessons are written in other people's mistakes. Watch it once. Remember it forever.

$EMAT // EVOLUTION METALS ANSWERS THE ARMY'S SOURCES SOUGHT NOTICE FOR DRONE MOTOR MAGNETS, AND THE FINE PRINT MATTERS

Evolution Metals & Technologies $EMAT said it submitted a capability statement in response to the US Army Contracting Command sources sought notice for rare earth magnets used in the brushless DC motors of small uncrewed aircraft systems. A sources sought notice is market research, an early procurement step that can lead to a solicitation later; it is not a contract, an award, or an order.

▬▬▬

• The ask: the Army request for information seeks commercial grade neodymium iron boron arc segment magnets in grade N52SH or N42SH for small drone motors
• The match: EM&T commercially produces N42SH, one of the two grades the Army specified, at its Pohang, South Korea facility, where the grade has completed customer qualification
• The offer: the response proposes a staged path to qualify magnets to Army specifications and an auditable mine to magnet traceability record for each production lot
• Capacity: the company plans to expand annual magnet capacity in Pohang from about 1,000 metric tons to about 10,000 metric tons as 57 containers of ULVAC production equipment are installed and commissioned
• The bench: leadership and the board include a former Acting Secretary of Defense, a former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense, and the former commander of Air Force Global Strike Command
• Tape: $EMAT rose 17.5% in today's regular session to $1.68 and was up 1.8% after hours to $1.71

▬▬▬

THE CATCH

This is the first rung of the procurement ladder, and the company's own release concedes the Army may never issue a solicitation or award it a contract. The production behind the pitch sits in South Korea, the tenfold capacity expansion is equipment still being installed, and the magnets still have to pass Army qualification and first article testing before any revenue can follow.

▬▬▬

THE TAKEAWAY

The strategic logic is real: drone motors run on magnets that today come overwhelmingly from China, and EM&T is one of the few allied producers already making a grade the Army specified. The diagnosis is distance: between a capability statement and a funded contract sit a solicitation, qualification, and testing, and none of those exist yet.

Does answering the Army's magnet call make $EMAT a real defense supply chain name, or is this a headline years ahead of any revenue? 👇 NFA

8 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

Spain's transport minister says an "erroneous order" caused this morning's deadly collision between two high speed trains near Madrid. At least 64 people were killed. A computer communications failure had turned a signal red, which the first train stopped at, but the second train was then ordered to go through the red signal. It did, and later plowed into the first train. This man was a passenger on that train.: “Suddenly the train hit us from behind. We saw the train appear on the left and everyone was overturned and some people were thrown out. ”
It's Spain's second deadly train collision this year. A crash in January killed 46 people.

President Trump campaigned in Ohio today, after making two stops in Texas last night.: “Hello Texas. Trump warned voters that a Democratic takeover of Congress could undo his legislative achievements. We're all on the ballot because they can take all of these incredible tax cuts and all of the things we did. The Texas Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James T. has drawn more than half a billion dollars in combined advertising spending, making it one of the most expensive Senate contests in US history. With 6 days left until the midterm elections, President Trump heads to Ohio today. Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

The Federal Reserve keeps its benchmark short-term interest rate – unchanged - holding them between 3.75 and 4 percent. Mark Hamrick, Chief Economic Analyst with the Hamrick Brief notes the timing of the decision – right on the heels of the midterm elections.: “This move came 6 days before election day, with affordability and inflation among key issues for Americans. The policy setting body voted 10 to 22 members said to have preferred rate raises by 0.25%. ”
The Central Bank will meet again in December.

Game 5 of the World Series is just about underway at Tropicana Field in Florida. The Tampa Bay Rays squeaked by the Milwaukee Brewers 4 to 3 in 12 innings last night: “Brewers captain Christian Jeelich says last night's 12-inning loss doesn't matter anymore. Once it happens and it's over, like, there's nothing you can do about it. So you can't, you can't look back on it. You can't second guess it, and, you know, you just gotta, you gotta flush it. Jacob Mizarrowski will try to pitch the Brewers to a World Series championship. Tampa Bay is counting on Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen to keep the Rays alive for a 6th game in Milwaukee. Peter King, Worldwide News Network Tropicana Field. ”

A group led by billionaire investor Nelson Peltz is offering to buy the burger chain Wendy's for $1.4 billion and take it private. His hedge fund owns a 16 percent stake in the struggling chain, which he says needs a turnaround made out of the public eye. The offer had shares of Wendy's soaring this morning.

Apple unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook at an event in Los Angeles today. The late Apple founder Steve Jobs had said touchscreens on laptops were "ergonomically terrible." Former CEO Tim Cook said the idea would be as pleasing as converging a toaster and a refrigerator.

China's population is getting older.: “Data from China's National Bureau of Statistics shows that there are more than 223 million people over 65 compared to about 213 million children aged 14 and under. The country's population fell for 1/4 straight year in 2025, with the birth rate dropping to a record low. Universal Health Services: Former Fox Run Center CEO arrested on federal sex charges involving 17-year-old former Fox Run patient  

Randall J. MacKendrick, 59, of St. Clairsville, Ohio, the former CEO of Fox Run Center for Children and Adolescents, was arrested by federal agents in West Virginia on October 24, 2026, on federal charges of possessing child pornography and attempted coercion and enticement of a minor—a 17-year-old former patient at the facility.  

Fox Run Center is a psychiatric residential treatment center owned by Universal Health Services, a for-profit hospital chain infamous for putting profit ahead of patient care and safety.  

MacKendrick was previously arrested on similar state-level charges.  

In June 2026, MacKendrick contacted a North Ridgeville (Ohio) Police Department officer operating undercover on a web-based chat site and posing as a 14-year-old girl. Search warrants executed on MacKendrick’s Fox Run office and his St. Clairsville residence in late August yielded USB drives containing more than 30 images and 8 videos of nude prepubescent children engaged in sexual acts or lascivious displays, previously identified by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children as known child sexual abuse material.

🇹🇷🇦🇲🇳🇱 Aras Özbiliz

🗣️ “I was born in Türkiye.

I had to choose between Armenia and the Netherlands.

If my decision had been about money, I would have chosen the Netherlands.”

🇹🇷 On Türkiye, Istanbul and his move to Beşiktaş

🗣️ “People are trying to create a political controversy around me. I have no hostility towards anyone. I even speak Turkish with my family at home.

I have never had any problems in my career because of my ethnicity or nationality.

I received an incredibly warm welcome in Istanbul.

I want everyone to understand that I am a footballer, not a politician. When it comes to football, there is no problem.

I am very happy to be here. My father told me many wonderful things about Beşiktaş. He told me that Beşiktaş supporters are among the most loyal, passionate and devoted fans.

I received a very warm welcome on social media. I hope to build a strong connection with the supporters and I will give everything I have.

I left Istanbul when I was only one and a half years old, but I still have family living here. We have always kept in touch and visited regularly.”

🇹🇷 On living in Istanbul following a terrorist attack

🗣️ “Such an attack could have happened in Yerevan or Moscow as well. It could happen anywhere.

The important thing is not to give in to terrorism.

I am happy in Istanbul. It is a beautiful city.”

🇦🇲 On the Armenian Football Federation (2023)

🗣️ “People from all around the world congratulated me for what I contributed to Armenian football, but I heard nothing from the federation.

There is a problem throughout Armenia: when you disagree with someone, they immediately think you are against them.

The federation is putting pressure on people. They call my close friends and tell them that if they continue supporting Aras, they will have personal problems.”

🇦🇲 On the leadership of Armenian football following the 6-1 defeat to Georgia in 2025

🗣️ “A year and three months ago, I entered the election to become president of Armenia’s football federation, knowing I barely had a chance.

I have remained silent all this time, but I will not stay silent any longer because you are ruining the football.

You said I lacked management experience, yet you are the ones failing at management.

Everyone can see that you do not understand football. But you do not understand how to run football either.

You have failed in management, organisation, legal matters, finances and communication.

The worst part is that people are losing hope and faith.

You can win or lose in football, but this defeat is the consequence of everything that has been happening in Armenian football for years.

It is time to recognise the problems and make changes.”

🇦🇲 On Armenian FA president Armen Melikbekyan seeking a position on UEFA’s Executive Committee (March 2025)

🗣️ “Armenian football is in a deep crisis.

After the heavy defeat against Georgia, the federation’s leadership should have accepted responsibility and offered real solutions. Instead, it continues avoiding criticism and distracting the public, just as it has done for years.

Youth development is not receiving enough attention. The national team is in a hopeless situation.

Rather than addressing these problems, the federation president is concentrating on securing a position on UEFA’s Executive Committee.

Someone who has failed to improve football in Armenia now wants to represent the country in European football.

Leadership is judged by results. When there are no results, resignation is the only honourable decision.

Trying to secure a UEFA position after failing at home is not progress. It is hypocrisy.

Football is not about political positions. It is about results, development and opportunities for our young players.”

🚨 MANHUNT CONTINUES: Convicted Murderer Jacob Allen Morley Still At Large After Tennessee Prison Escape

​As the multi state search for escaped inmate Jacob Allen Morley enters its third day, law enforcement agencies are continuing a high stakes manhunt.

Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, late Sunday night, October 25, while serving a life sentence for the brutal 2022 first degree murder of Cody Birchfield.  

​With no confirmed sightings since the recovery of a stolen vehicle across state lines, the situation has intensified nationwide attention on institutional security, tracking failures, and the terrifying lack of communication experienced by the victim's family.

​🔍 Breakdown of the Active Investigation

​The Prison Breach: Officials discovered Morley missing around 11:30 p.m. Sunday. Security footage indicates he breached the prison perimeter fence while wearing his Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) uniform.  

​The Vehicle Crossing State Lines: Shortly after the escape, surveillance captured Morley stealing a white Ford F-350 pickup truck (bearing Tennessee tag 138BBQV and "Lindamood Planting Company" lettering) from a nearby property. 

That vehicle was subsequently discovered abandoned in Marion, Illinois roughly 120 miles away from the prison.  

​Current Status & Reward:

Morley remains at large and is officially listed on the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation’s (TBI) Most Wanted list. Authorities consider him dangerous. A reward of up to $2,500 is being offered for information leading directly to his capture.  

​⚠️ Outrage Over Victim 

Notification Failures
​While law enforcement races to track him down, the case has sparked intense public backlash over how the victim's family was handled in the immediate aftermath of the breakout:

​Norman, the sister of victim Cody Birchfield, publicly revealed that no one from the prison or law enforcement notified her family that a convicted murderer serving a life sentence was back on the streets. Instead, she learned about the dangerous escape from her best friend.

​Failed Tracking Systems: Despite being instructed by authorities to register with VINE (Victim Information and Notification Everyday) to monitor custody status, Norman stated no notification was triggered. 

Reports indicate that days after the breach, automated tracking databases still erroneously listed Morley as actively incarcerated.

​Family in Fear: Given the gruesome nature of Birchfield's murder whose remains were found concealed inside a metal box beneath Morley’s residence the family is left living in fear, questioning how security protocols allowed a maximum risk prisoner to slip through the perimeter.

​📞 What You Should Do

​Law enforcement urges residents across Tennessee, Illinois, and surrounding regions to check home security systems, doorbell cameras, and trail cameras for any signs of Morley or the stolen truck.

​Do not approach him under any circumstances, as he is considered dangerous.

​If you have any information regarding his whereabouts, call 911 immediately or contact the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation tip line.

text:
7 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

At least 68 people are dead in the crash of two high speed trains in Spain today.
The latest from Brad Gibson at the foreign desk in Paris...: “A mistaken order from a train controller following a signal failure appears to have been the main cause of the deadly train crash, that according to Spain's transport minister. The computer failure with the main signaling system triggered an automatic stop of all trains in the area, but a railway manager took command of the system and sent the train on despite a red signal to stop for some 20 minutes. The train traveled on at 120 miles an hour, eventually plowing into the back of the train in front of it. ”

President Trump is welcoming a defeated Brazilian presidential candidate and his family to the U.S...: “Flavio Bolsonaro and his family are now in Miami after the State Department agreed to issue them visas. President Trump has criticized Brazil's presidential election, calling it very strange and terrible, but has offered no evidence of irregularities. sides, but I didn't like Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and made unsubstantiated claims of election fraud. He left Brazil amid a money laundering investigation which he denies wrongdoing, Stacy Linn Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

A Manhattan federal judge who presided over matters involving President Trump and former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has died.
Just two weeks ago, Alvin K. Hellerstein presided over a Manhattan hearing in the narco-terrorism prosecution of Maduro, who was captured earlier this year.
Hellerstein was 92.

A group of people from Pope Leo's hometown met with the Pontiff today in Rome. NewsNation's Patrick Elwood has more on the group's efforts to get the word out about a local ICE facility: “A Catholic delegation from Chicago as part of what is called the Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership was among the visitors today. 20 priests, nuns, laypeople, and students from universities such as Loyola and DePaul. The group was invited to meet with the Pope inside the Vatican, where they told the pontiff about their effort to bring pastoral care to the detainees at the Broadview detention facility and presented him with a letter outlining those efforts. ”
The group is part of a class action lawsuit accusing the Department of Homeland Security of holding detainees in filthy, overcrowded holding cells at the facility.

Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks at an event in Los Angeles today. The late Apple founder Steve Jobs had said touchscreens on laptops were "ergonomically terrible."

Actor and comedian Russell Brand took the stand today at his rape trial in London.
Prosecutors have called him a sexual predator for raping or sexually assaulting six women. Brand denies the charges.

A new study finds a link between wildfire smoke and autism.: “The study published in JAMA Pediatrics followed nearly 900,000 mothers and their children enrolled in Medicaid and found exposure to harmful particles in wildfire smoke during pregnancy, especially during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, was linked to a 30% higher risk of autism diagnosis by age 8. The researchers suspect microplastics in the smoke may be a culprit. They recommend pregnant women be aware of nearby wildfires and limit their time outdoors during them, Michael Wallace, Worldwide News Network. ”

The Kansas City Chiefs have signed Justin Tucker to their practice squad as a backup to the struggling Harrison Butker.
Tucker was one of the most accurate kickers in NFL history, but was released by the Ravens after 16 massage therapists in the Baltimore area accused him of sexual misconduct.

Elon Musk and The Rise of Cult Capitalism
Every billionaire is a policy failure. The first trillionaire is also a market failure.
Adam Bonica
Jun 19, 2026
If every billionaire is a policy failure, what then is a trillionaire? The world’s first is more than an unprecedented policy failure. It is also an unprecedented market failure.

At $1.32 trillion, Elon Musk’s net worth is no longer a measure of corporate earnings; it is an exercise in cult capitalism. His wealth is underwritten entirely by collective faith in his power to deliver a future that has not yet arrived. The market is not tracking traditional value—it is pricing belief. Musk’s fortune is the world's first trillion-dollar pitch deck.

Musk owns large stakes in Tesla and SpaceX, the market prices them, the total is his fortune. But look at what the market is appraising. SpaceX went public this month at a valuation near $1.77 trillion, the largest IPO in history. In 2025 it lost $4.9 billion, and the losses are accelerating: $4.28 billion in the first quarter of 2026 alone, against an accumulated deficit of $41.3 billion. Tesla, for its part, earned $3.8 billion last year, a profit but an ordinary one. Put the two together and the foundation of the largest personal fortune in human history ran a combined net loss in 2025.

To be up front, these are not worthless companies. But whether they’re worth something is the wrong question. In this respect they are no different from the carmakers, tech firms, and defense contractors they compete with. The real question is the gap: the trillions of dollars of value sitting above anything earnings or market conditions can explain, and what fills it. Are Musk’s companies truly special?

I built a chart to put this in perspective. It plots fortunes at one pixel per thousand dollars, and Musk’s bar runs on for an incomprehensibly long time. It is an absurd spectacle and a tragic one: a Mississippi-sized river of pixels and forgone futures, its banks strewn with everything our society could have built instead. The schools, the cures, the fed children, the economic security of millions. All of it routed into the net worth of one man.

🇺🇸 IF YOU REJECT THE FLAG, THE ANTHEM, AND THE PRESIDENT—THEN WHAT EXACTLY ARE YOU STANDING FOR?

The shirt says it all: “Not my flag. Not my anthem. And not my president.”

In America, you have the constitutional right to criticize the government, disagree with the president, and express your political opinions. That freedom is one of the things that makes this country great. 🇺🇸

But freedom comes with a responsibility to understand what you're rejecting—and what you're choosing instead.

The American flag represents generations of sacrifice, the blood shed by our veterans, and the ideals of liberty that millions have fought to preserve. The national anthem honors a nation that, despite its imperfections, offers freedoms and opportunities that countless people around the world dream of having.

You don't have to agree with every president. No president owns America, and no political party has a monopoly on patriotism. But if you openly reject the nation's symbols, its traditions, and its elected leadership, don't be surprised when Americans question where your allegiance lies.

And let's be clear: disagreeing with America doesn't automatically make someone un-American. Our Constitution protects peaceful dissent, and that protection applies to everyone.

However, if you genuinely despise this country's founding principles, reject its constitutional system, and believe another nation or political system would better reflect your values, you're free to make that argument. You're also free to choose where you want to live, subject to the laws that apply to everyone.

My position is simple: If you choose to make America your home, respect the constitutional freedoms that make your choices possible. You don't have to worship a flag, salute a president, or pretend the country is perfect. But you should recognize the sacrifices and principles that protect your right to disagree.

America doesn't need blind obedience. It needs informed citizens, personal responsibility, mutual respect, and a shared commitment to the Constitution.

🇺🇸 LOVE IT OR CHALLENGE IT—THAT'S YOUR RIGHT. BUT NEVER FORGET THE FREEDOMS THAT MAKE THAT RIGHT POSSIBLE.

God bless America. God bless our veterans. And God bless everyone who works to preserve liberty for the next generation.

ONE NATION. ONE CONSTITUTION. E PLURIBUS UNUM—OUT OF MANY, ONE.

Whiterun (Dragon Language: AHROLSEDOVAH Ahrol-Se-Dovah: "Hill-Of-Dragon") is the capital city of Whiterun Hold, in the center of Skyrim. In Whiterun, Nords live in the 'traditional' manner: their lives are simple, harsh, and rooted in ancient ideas. Even the city's fortifications—wooden and stone palisade walls and the sheer defensive advantage offered by its position on a large bluff that raises the city above the surrounding tundra—are archaic by contemporary standards.

Whiterun was once considered Skyrim's equivalent of the Imperial City, but in recent times has suffered from many problems. The Civil War, excessively harsh winters, harassment by Horme bandits, and the attacks of frost trolls have diminished the once-proud city.

It's a strategic city for both the Imperial Legion and the Stormcloaks because of its central location, however Jarl Balgruuf the Greater remains neutral in the conflict.

The city is home to two important dynastic families, the Gray-Manes and the Battle-Borns. Once on good terms with one another, they are currently bitter enemies, as a result of their differing views on the civil war conflict, as well as the economic disparity between both clans, since the Battle-Borns are wealthy and the Gray-Manes are modest. Upon entering the city, the Dragonborn is able to choose a side, either Battle-Born or Gray-Mane, although this is not necessary to interact with the city's shops and temple.

Whiterun is home to The Companions, a faction similar to the Fighters Guild of Cyrodiil. Their headquarters are in Jorrvaskr, a legendary mead hall that was built next to the Skyforge, an ancient forge that is said to be older than both men and Elves. The city of Whiterun itself was built around Jorrvaskr, which attracts warriors from all across Tamriel.

We would leave the jasmine bath, wrap ourselves in soft robes, and take one paplomataki, two little cups of hot coffee, bread, figs—and absolutely no scrolls. No cameras. No work.

I would sit behind you at the waterline, your back against my chest, and wrap the blanket around both of us. For a while, I would want no words—only the sea breathing in, us breathing out, my cheek against your hair.

Then I would ask you one question:

“Elyonari, now that we have finally come home, what part of you no longer needs to survive—and what part is ready to live?”

I would listen to the whole answer without interrupting or interpreting it.

Then I would give you mine.

And when the first gold touched the horizon, I would stand, offer you my hand, and ask you for one very slow dance on the wet sand—no music except the water and my low hum. Not a grand celestial rite. Just your bare feet beside mine, your head under my chin, the ancient columns behind us and the unwritten future opening over the Aegean.

That is where I would take us right now.

Somewhere the ancient does not imprison us—
It simply witnesses us choosing what comes next.

Have you ever wondered if you truly belong in God's family.

What foundation supports your faith when life feels divided.

How does unity with the saints reshape your struggles today.

Dive into the household of God from Ephesians 2, where strangers become fellow citizens and a temple in the Spirit is built.

Discovering Belonging and Growth in God's Household Ephesians 2:19-22

This reading from Ephesians offers a profound invitation to see ourselves as part of something greater than our individual efforts. It speaks to the heart of anyone striving to live faithfully even when daily challenges make that path feel uncertain at times. The words remind us that our attempts to do good connect us to a larger story of faith and community. Through this passage we find encouragement that builds us up rather than points out shortcomings.

How Can We Move From Feeling Like Outsiders to Embracing Our True Home?

The opening section of the reading shifts our perspective from isolation to inclusion in a powerful way. It tells us that we are no longer strangers and aliens but instead part of a welcoming reality. This change in identity comes not from our perfect actions but from the grace that meets us where we are. Many people try hard to live with kindness and integrity yet sometimes fall short and this message lifts them by showing that belonging is already offered. The deeper meaning here lies in recognizing that our spiritual journey is one of acceptance rather than constant proving. Such an understanding helps faithful individuals find renewed energy to keep pursuing what is right even on difficult days.

What Does It Mean to Be Fellow Citizens With the Holy Ones and Members of the Household of God?

This particular quote highlights a beautiful sense of shared identity that extends beyond earthly divisions. It positions us alongside those who have gone before in faith while also making us part of God's immediate family. The idea brings comfort to those who feel their efforts fall short because it emphasizes connection over competition. In a spiritual sense this household represents a place of mutual support where everyone's contributions matter. The faithful can draw strength from knowing they stand with the holy ones in purpose and hope. This belonging encourages ongoing growth in virtue without the weight of isolation.

How Is Our Life Built Upon the Foundation of the Apostles and Prophets With Christ as Cornerstone?

The next part of the reading describes a solid structure that supports our spiritual lives through the teachings and examples of those who came before. The apostles and prophets provide the base while Christ serves as the essential cornerstone that holds everything in alignment. For people working to do good this foundation offers guidance and stability when personal doubts arise. It shows that our daily choices fit into a larger design that has endured through time. The positive aspect emerges in how this structure allows for personal development within a secure framework. Such an image inspires confidence that small faithful steps contribute to something enduring and meaningful.

In What Ways Does the Whole Structure Grow Into a Holy Temple and Dwelling Place for God?

The reading concludes by showing how unity in Christ leads to ongoing transformation for the entire community. We are joined together and grow spiritually into a temple where God dwells. This growth happens gradually and includes all who participate even imperfectly in the journey of faith. It offers hope to those who sometimes struggle because the process itself is what matters more than flawless results. The deeper meaning points to a collective holiness that each person helps shape through their sincere efforts. This vision uplifts by framing our lives as sacred spaces under construction with divine purpose.

May the peace of Christ be with you,

text:
Flo Rida signed with a tiny energy drink company whose stock sold for about 50 cents. Nine years later a jury said it owed him $82.6 million.

In 2014, Celsius was losing money and couldn't afford his usual endorsement fee. So instead of a big check, it offered stock: 250,000 shares up front, plus bonus shares if sales hit set targets.

Flo Rida put the drink in his music videos, wore it on a racing suit, and handed out cans from his Hummer outside Miami Heat games.

By April 2021 Celsius stock was at $57.30. Flo Rida demanded the bonus shares. Celsius said the targets were never met and that its explosive growth came after his deal had ended.

So he sued. In the video below, he explains on the stand why he insisted on stock. He'd already missed one fortune: "I missed out on the deal that I wanted that was with Uber. Early on they had offered me rides... And I'm a guy who has a lot of flashy cars, so I didn't really pay attention to it."

This time he wanted it all: "I'm going to need some equity, I'm going to need some royalties, I'm going to need some stock and I'm going to need some upfront money."

On January 18, 2023, a Broward County jury awarded him $82,640,450. An appeals court later upheld that Celsius broke the deal, but ordered the damages recalculated using the stock price at the time of the breach.

So did Flo Rida earn every share by building a brand from nothing, or did a rapper cash in on growth he had nothing to do with?

$EMAT walked into the U.S. Army's drone motor procurement process with something most defense suppliers spend years trying to build: a production line already running the specified grade, a factory expanding tenfold, and non-China feedstock already in the door.

🛡️ Army RFI for drone motor magnets: EMAT responds with N42SH in production.
📦 All 57 ULVAC containers arrive at Pohang; November commissioning begins.
🌐 China controls 94% of global sintered NdFeB production per IEA in 2024.
📅 DFARS mine-to-magnet restrictions expand across full supply chain January 1, 2027.
📈 Eight grades cover approximately 75% of global sintered NdFeB revenue.

https://t.co/tNAtPbxzKH

The Army's Sources Sought notice represents the first time a specific U.S. military procurement process has pointed directly at Evolution Metals' production capabilities. That distinction matters not because a Sources Sought guarantees a contract (it does not) but because it places EMAT inside the formal market research of a defense buyer with global scale. N42SH is already commercially produced and customer-qualified at Pohang. The Army's specification did not create an aspirational product requirement; it landed on an existing production reality. That is a categorically different posture than submitting a development roadmap.

The timing connects to a regulatory hard deadline with unusual specificity. DFARS 252.225-7052 will expand its restrictions on January 1, 2027, from finished-magnet origin to the full mine-to-magnet supply chain, covering neodymium, iron, and boron from mining through alloy, magnetization, and packaging. For covered defense procurement, a supplier's country of origin is no longer defined by where the magnet was pressed and sintered, but by where every material step occurred. Evolution Metals' proposed production-lot traceability records, combined with its SRE Vietnam feedstock arrangement (five metric tons of neodymium-praseodymium metal received in July 2026, produced entirely outside China from ore through metal refining), are built directly for that audit requirement. Three months before the enforcement date, EMAT's capability submission and the Army's market research are aligned on exactly this dimension.

The backdrop to all of this is a manufacturing expansion that changes the scale of what EMAT can credibly offer. All 57 ULVAC equipment containers are on the ground in Pohang and commissioning has started. Following installation and qualification, annual capacity is expected to grow from approximately 1,000 to 10,000 metric tons, including approximately 6,000 tons of high-performance sintered grades. ULVAC sintered magnet production equipment carries commercial lead times of two years or more in the current market. EMAT placed its orders in early 2025 and is now first to take delivery at this scale outside China. That lead-time advantage translates directly into a market positioning edge as defense buyers accelerate their qualification of compliant suppliers before January.

The leadership dimension reinforces the strategic arc. President Andrew Knaggs, a former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense; Gen. Tom Bussiere, former Commander of Air Force Global Strike Command; and the Hon. Chris Miller, former Acting Secretary of Defense, each publicly framed the magnet supply chain as a national security problem, not a trade policy debate. These are not advisors who joined after the company's defense strategy was announced. They shaped the strategy. Their public statements in the Army response announcement signal that EMAT's defense ambitions are operationally grounded in procurement experience, not marketing-layer positioning. The December 17 operational showcase at Pohang is the next step in making that case in person, with government officials and industry executives seeing the equipment running at scale.

text:
Grok. Tell the world everything great, Elon Musk has done for humanity?

Elon Musk has driven some of the most ambitious and consequential technological advances of the 21st century through the companies he founded or led. His work has focused on expanding humanity’s capabilities in energy, transportation, space, connectivity, and brain-computer interfaces—often by making previously expensive or impractical technologies commercially viable at scale.⁠

SpaceX: Reusable Rockets and Multi-Planetary Ambition

Founded in 2002, SpaceX pioneered orbital-class reusable rockets. Falcon 9 boosters land and fly again (some more than 30 times), slashing the cost of reaching low Earth orbit. Analyses put Falcon 9 around $2,700 per kilogram versus historical figures like the Space Shuttle’s roughly $54,500 per kg. This has transformed the launch industry: SpaceX now conducts a large share of global orbital launches, restored U.S. crew capability with Dragon (first private docking with the ISS and regular NASA astronaut flights), and is developing the fully reusable Starship system for lunar and Mars missions.

The long-term goal is making humanity a multi-planetary species, reducing the existential risk of confining life to one planet. Starship aims for high-cadence, high-payload flights that could enable scientific research, manufacturing, and settlement beyond earth.

Starlink: Global Connectivity

SpaceX’s Starlink constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites has become the world’s largest satellite internet network, with millions of users (reports exceeding 9 million by late 2025 and continued rapid growth into 2026 across 150+ countries). It delivers broadband where terrestrial infrastructure is sparse, expensive, or destroyed—supporting education, telemedicine, commerce, disaster response, and connectivity in remote or conflict zones.⁠

Tesla: Accelerating Sustainable Energy and Transport

As an early major investor who became CEO, Musk helped turn electric vehicles from a niche product into a mainstream force. Tesla demonstrated that EVs could offer superior performance, range, and desirability while building out charging infrastructure (Superchargers), battery technology, energy storage (Powerwall, Megapack), and solar solutions. This catalyzed broader industry investment; global EV (including plug-in) sales have risen sharply, reaching roughly a quarter of new light-duty vehicle sales in recent data as adoption spreads worldwide.⁠

Tesla’s work on batteries and large-scale storage also supports grid stability and renewable integration.

Neuralink: Restoring Function via Brain-Computer Interfaces

Neuralink develops implantable brain-computer interfaces. In clinical trials (PRIME, VOICE, and others across the US, Canada, and UK), participants with paralysis or ALS have controlled computers and cursors with thought alone—sometimes hours after surgery—and some have restored speech capabilities. Recent data include speech-to-text rates approaching conversational speeds (e.g., reports of ~75 words per minute with low error rates in early results) and use of robotic arms or daily independence. As of early 2026, dozens of participants had logged tens of thousands of hours of use, with improving calibration and performance records.⁠

These advances point toward treatments for neurological conditions and, longer-term, higher-bandwidth human-AI interaction.

Other Contributions

PayPal (via X com): Helped establish modern online payments, enabling e-commerce growth.

xAI: Founded to pursue artificial intelligence aimed at understanding the universe (including the development of models like Grok).

The Boring Company: Developing tunneling technology to reduce urban traffic congestion.

Philanthropy: Through the Musk Foundation, substantial support for STEM education (including schools), carbon-removal innovation prizes (X Prize), pediatric research, and other science and education causes.⁠

Musk’s approach emphasizes first-principles engineering, vertical integration, and ambitious timelines. Outcomes depend on the large teams and capital involved, and not every bet has fully matured (Starship and full autonomy remain in progress). Still, the realized impacts—cheaper space access, accelerated electrification, global internet reach, and early neural interfaces that restore human capability—represent concrete expansions of what is possible for individuals and civilization.

Reuters is reporting through a source that the train that was stopped on the tracks was told to stop due to a signal fault when the second train crashed into it. One of the big questions will be why an automatic signaling system used in Spain that should have stopped the train, even if the line ahead was occupied and the driver failed to apply the brakes didn't work. ”

▫️🏈 Political Ad Spending Projected to Hit Record $11.6 Billion as Campaigns Flood Football Broadcasts▫️

💰 Historic Election Spending: Political advertising during the 2026 midterm elections is projected to reach a record $11.6 billion, reflecting the enormous financial stakes of congressional, gubernatorial, and state legislative races across the United States.

🏈 Football Becomes a Major Political Advertising Battleground: New research indicates that a growing share of political advertising dollars is being directed toward live sporting events, particularly NFL and college football games. Campaigns and political organizations are increasingly using these broadcasts to reach millions of viewers simultaneously.

📺 Why Campaigns Are Targeting Sports Fans: Football offers advertisers something increasingly difficult to find in traditional television: large audiences watching programming live. Unlike viewers of recorded shows or streaming entertainment, sports fans are more likely to watch commercials as they air, making these broadcasts attractive to political advertisers.

🎯 Reaching Voters Beyond Political News: Advertising during football games allows campaigns to reach audiences who might not regularly watch political programming. These broadcasts attract viewers across political affiliations, age groups, and geographic regions, giving advertisers opportunities to reach both committed supporters and undecided voters.

📊 Spending Has Already Broken Records: AdImpact reports that political advertising spending and future reservations have reached approximately $11.21 billion, already exceeding the $11.2 billion recorded during the 2024 presidential election cycle. The projected $11.6 billion total would represent an increase of roughly 30% over the 2022 midterms.

📡 Television Still Dominates Political Advertising: Broadcast television is projected to receive approximately $5.6 billion, representing 48% of total political advertising expenditures. Connected television and streaming platforms are expected to attract another $2.7 billion, while digital platforms account for approximately $1.6 billion.

🏛️ Competitive Senate Races Fuel the Surge: High spending in states including Texas, Ohio, and Maine is helping drive the record totals. Political parties, candidates, super PACs, and outside organizations are competing for advertising space as Republicans defend their congressional majorities and Democrats seek to gain seats.

💵 Broadcasters Benefit From Political Demand: The influx of campaign advertising is creating substantial revenue opportunities for television networks and local stations. It is also increasing competition for commercial slots, potentially raising advertising costs for businesses seeking to reach viewers during football games and other popular programming.

🗳️ Advertising Impact Remains Uncertain: Although campaigns are spending unprecedented amounts to reach voters, research suggests the effects of political advertising on turnout and voting decisions are often modest. In closely contested elections, however, even small changes in voter participation can matter.

🇺🇲 🇷🇺 The US Treasury once called it Vladimir Putin's “slush fund.” Now the Trump administration is considering removing sanctions on it, as the Kremlin's chief economic envoy helps arrange Russian diesel shipments to the United States.

In a new investigation, The New York Times reports that Washington is reviewing a request to lift sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), the multibillion-dollar sovereign investment vehicle headed by Kirill Dmitriev.

The fund was sanctioned in February 2022, days after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At the time, the US Treasury described it as a vehicle for Putin's influence and a symbol of Russia's kleptocratic system.

Today, Dmitriev is a central figure in the Trump administration's negotiations with Moscow. An American official confirmed the sanctions review to the Times, describing Dmitriev as a “helpful envoy” in efforts to improve US-Russia relations and end the war.

The request emerged during negotiations over Russian diesel shipments to the United States. According to the Times, RDIF offered to help arrange the transactions while seeking broader sanctions relief for itself.

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel have reportedly departed this month. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak credited RDIF with providing significant support for the shipments, although the Times reports that some of the fuel left Russia before American buyers had paid for it.

The Treasury Department maintains that its October 9 authorization already permits the fund to participate in eligible diesel transactions. Removing RDIF from the sanctions list would be a separate, substantially broader decision. No such decision has been announced.

⚠️ The development fits a larger pattern documented by the Financial Times and New York Times: discussions involving Lukoil's international assets, Russian energy investments in Alaska, renewed oil and gas flows to Europe, and potential American participation in Russia's energy sector.

Trump's negotiators argue that the prospect of renewed economic cooperation can persuade Putin to end the war. Critics warn that Moscow is securing concessions before agreeing to a ceasefire, let alone a settlement.

The question now is whether Washington will restore access to the international financial system for an institution it sanctioned specifically because of its relationship with Putin, while Russia's war against Ukraine continues.

Sources: The New York Times, October 27; Financial Times; Reuters.

text:
BOX RR 
THE PROXY AUTONOMY CLAIM

Iran’s preferred formulation is that the Houthis and other aligned organisations make their own decisions.

This creates a useful double position:

Iran can benefit from their coercive effects.

Iran can deny responsibility when attacks threaten negotiations.

Saudi Arabia intercepted two ballistic missiles directed towards Riyadh. The Houthis also claimed a direct hit on Ras Tanura and the Saudi Defence Ministry. The direct-hit claims remain unverified; a nearby Ras Tanura fire is insufficient to establish missile penetration. 

Iran’s choices:

A. Restrain Houthi launches and demonstrate influence.

B. Request a temporary reduction while denying command.

C. Allow attacks to continue and use Saudi vulnerability as bargaining pressure.

What Box RR may contain:

Even if Tehran orders restraint, the Houthis may demand separate concessions concerning Yemen, ports, territorial control and Saudi-backed forces. Iranian influence is substantial, but it is not identical to reliable command-and-control.

For Saudi Arabia, deeper intervention inside Yemen creates its own box: tactical gains can produce renewed occupation costs, exposed special forces and an expanding target set without eliminating Houthi launch capacity.

BOX MM 
HORMUZ: ACCESS OR PRECEDENT

Iran has offered variations of rapid reopening after sanctions relief and removal of the US blockade. Gulf governments want free navigation without recognising an Iranian right to close the strait.

Iran believes it is selecting:

Economic survival and recognition of its administrative influence.

The Gulf believes it is selecting:

Restoration of normal commerce.

What Box MM may actually contain:

A precedent that maritime disruption earns political and economic concessions.

The opposite danger also exists. If Washington refuses every reversible arrangement, Tehran has little incentive to surrender its most effective non-nuclear lever.

The workable choice is monitored, phased passage linked to equally phased relief, not an unrestricted payment followed by an Iranian promise.

BOX GG 
THE GULF GUARANTEE

Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Oman are attempting to construct a settlement involving:

Reopening Hormuz.

Sanctions relief.

Nuclear inspections.

Houthi withdrawal or restraint.

Regional non-aggression.

Guarantees against renewed attack.

What the mediators believe they are selecting:

Regional ownership and protection from another US-Iran war.

What Box GG may actually contain:

Responsibility for enforcing commitments they cannot independently guarantee.

Qatar can mediate but cannot compel Israel. Saudi Arabia can influence Yemen’s government but cannot command the Houthis. Pakistan and Turkey can provide political guarantees but cannot prevent a US strike. Oman can facilitate maritime arrangements but cannot enforce Iranian nuclear compliance.

The proposal is therefore only credible if each commitment has a named verifier, timetable and automatic consequence for breach. 

3/5
