text:
BOX EE 
UNITED STATES: THE “SHORT, INTENSE” WAR

Washington’s choices:

A. Conduct a concentrated post-election strike against nuclear, missile, command and infrastructure targets.

B. Maintain the blockade and sanctions while keeping military forces prepared.

C. Exchange limited sanctions relief for verified Iranian concessions.

What Washington believes it is selecting through renewed strikes:

Further degradation, restored deterrence and sufficient pressure to force Tehran into a weaker negotiation.

What Box EE may actually contain:

Iranian attacks on Gulf energy facilities, US bases, shipping, undersea infrastructure and allied interests outside the immediate theatre. Further bombing could destroy visible infrastructure without locating nuclear material or changing Iran’s political decision-making.

The United States has reportedly reinforced Israeli missile defence, replenished munitions and dispersed personnel from exposed bases. These actions create a credible option but do not prove a decision. 

The central error would be confusing operational brevity with strategic closure. The bombing phase may be short; the retaliation and force-protection burden would not be.

BOX JJ 
ISRAEL: THE CARETAKER GAMBLE

With 88.6% counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected at 53 seats, Eisenkot’s Jewish-led opposition at 48 and Arab-led parties at 19. Neither principal bloc reaches the 61-seat majority. Netanyahu therefore remains caretaker and has the strongest starting position, but no independent mandate to begin an open-ended war. 

Netanyahu’s choices:

A. Strike before coalition negotiations constrain him.

B. Wait for the United States and preserve Israeli defences.

C. Use the Iranian threat to attract additional coalition partners.

What Netanyahu believes he may be selecting through limited action:

Strategic initiative, electoral authority and destruction of Iranian capabilities before they can be rebuilt.

What Box JJ may actually contain:

A caretaker government committing Israel to a wider conflict whose political costs must be carried by a coalition that does not yet exist.

The election does not automatically make war more likely. It creates two opposing pressures:

Netanyahu has an incentive to demonstrate control and frame coalition negotiations around national security.

He also lacks a majority and would be vulnerable if an elective operation caused heavy retaliation or failed to deliver a clear result.

The most likely Israeli choice is therefore not an immediate independent strategic war. It is continued preparation, intelligence collection and pressure on Washington, with limited action possible if new intelligence supplies an operational justification.

Eisenkot’s bloc does not offer strategic accommodation with Iran. A change of prime minister could alter sequencing and consultation with Washington, but not Israel’s rejection of an Iranian nuclear-weapons capability.

2/5

text:
BERTRAND’S BOX 
28 OCTOBER 2026
IRAN–LEVANT–GULF–US AND ALLIES

STRATEGIC JUDGEMENT

The confrontation has reached a choice point, but the boxes are being mislabelled.

Washington’s box is marked “short, decisive campaign.” 

Tehran’s is marked “regional peace.” 

Israel’s is marked “preventive security.” 

The Gulf box is marked “guaranteed settlement.” 

None necessarily contains what its label promises.

Iran currently holds the asymmetric initiative because it can distribute pressure across Hormuz, Yemen, Saudi energy infrastructure, Iraqi actors, maritime insurance, cyber systems and proxy networks. 

The United States and Israel retain decisive conventional superiority, but superiority is being neutralised by uncertainty over political outcomes, missing nuclear material and the location of Iranian retaliation.

The next 24–72 hours are more likely to produce coercive positioning than a decisive strike. 

The decisive deadline is the US midterm election on 3 November, after which Washington’s freedom of action expands.

EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE

Confirmed:

Washington is preparing military options, but no strike decision has been announced.

Qatar has presented a seven-day framework; Iran calls the ideas unacceptable but remains engaged.

Israel’s election has produced no governing majority.

Saudi Arabia intercepted ballistic missiles directed towards Riyadh.

A fire occurred near Ras Tanura; the Houthi claim of a direct refinery hit remains unverified.

IAEA inspectors still cannot verify Iran’s sensitive nuclear stockpile.

Credible but unverified:

Washington has reportedly warned Gulf governments to prepare for a short, intense post-election campaign.

Russian space-based intelligence may be improving Iranian-aligned targeting.

Iran may be prepared to reopen Hormuz rapidly if sanctions and the US blockade are lifted.

Assessment:

Iran, Washington and Israel are all preserving the option to escalate while attempting to make the other side responsible for diplomatic failure.

THE BOXES

BOX II 
IRAN: THE REVERSIBLE CONCESSION

Tehran’s choices:

A. Accept the Gulf framework, reopen Hormuz and permit inspections.

B. Offer limited maritime access while retaining the ability to close it again.

C. Reject the proposal and prepare for renewed US-Israeli strikes.

What Iran believes it is selecting:

Sanctions relief, protection from attack, continued regional influence and recognition that Hormuz cannot be secured without Iranian consent.

What Box II may actually contain:

Inspection of damaged nuclear facilities, scrutiny of the unverified enriched-uranium stockpile, pressure to restrain the Houthis and a snapback mechanism that removes sanctions relief after any breach.

Iran is therefore unlikely to surrender all its leverage at once. Its most rational choice is a reversible concession: limited safe passage, temporary Houthi reduction and continued negotiations without abandoning maritime control.

1/5

14 Oct 2026

Should you publish your content as a PDF or stick strictly to standard HTML?

Does Google treat PDF files differently when it comes to indexing, ranking, and AI search features?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team demystify how Google Search handles PDF documents.

They break down some of Google's internal pipelines, explain why putting an LLMs.txt file inside a PDF is a bad idea, explore common technical traps like rasterized pages and canonicalization issues, and share practical advice on managing PDFs for SEO, AEO (SEO), and user experience.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   Google's PDF converter pipeline: How Google converts binary PDF containers into HTML pages during indexing so the rest of the pipeline can process them normally.

LLMs.txt as a PDF: Why saving an LLMs.txt file as a PDF is a bad idea, even if you like LLMs.txt.     File limits & Project Gutenberg: Why crawling limits exist, and how HTML and PDF size limits function in the crawl pipeline.

Rasterized pages & accessibility: How pages saved as images destroy text readability, ruin screen reader accessibility, and prevent Google from extracting text content.

Canonicalization & "binary blobs": Why identical PDF downloads across different sites make canonicalization harder and how using rel="canonical" HTTP headers or embedded header links can help.

PDFs for SEO in AI Overviews: How PDFs are parsed, ranked, and referenced in Google Search, AI Overviews, and broader AI systems for training and grounding.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

HTML is preferred, and PDFs work: HTML offers better mobile responsiveness, zoom reflow, and faster loading.

Internally, Google converts indexable PDF text into HTML so they can rank normally and appear in AI features.

Test for text indexability: Highlight and copy text out of your PDF into a text editor; if text doesn't copy, it might be a rasterized image and can't be indexed easily.

For restaurant menus: A PDF menu is better than no menu at all for restaurants, but a responsive HTML web page provides superior performance, accessibility, and user experience. (Credit: Google)

Do sitemaps still matter?
https://t.co/alBGitJS19

1 October 2026

Sitemaps have been a core element of web development and search engine optimization for two decades, yet Search Console warnings like "Couldn't fetch" continue to generate concern among site owners.

Are XML sitemaps still necessary with modern search crawlers, or can search engines and AI bots figure out site structure on their own?

In this episode of Search off the Record, Google Search Relations team members Martin Splitt and John Mueller break down the history, technical specifications, and some misconceptions surrounding sitemaps, RSS feeds, LLMs.txt, canonicalization signals, and Search Console indexing behaviors.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Origins of Sitemaps: How early web crawling challenges led to the sitemap standard and how building a sitemap generator started John Mueller's career at Google.

Obsolete vs. Active XML Fields: Why Google dropped support for the priority and changefreq tags, and how the lastmod date is actually evaluated.

XML Sitemaps vs. RSS Feeds: How RSS feeds function as lightweight sitemaps for recent updates and why AI training crawlers utilize both.     Technical Limits & Index Files: The exact URL (50,000) and file size (50MB uncompressed) limits, alongside best practices for sitemap index files and robots.txt declarations.

HTML Sitemaps & LLMs.txt: Why user-facing HTML maps and Markdown-based LLMs.txt files cannot replace structured XML sitemaps for search engines.     Troubleshooting "Couldn't Fetch": How host load management and perceived site quality (crawl demand) trigger non-technical fetching errors in Search Console.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

Keep Sitemaps Enabled by Default: Even for small websites or dynamic CMS setups, keeping auto-generated sitemaps active carries no downside and assists with discovery as sites grow.

Provide Accurate lastmod Timestamps: Avoid setting all page timestamps to the current date; Google evaluates date reliability and will ignore lastmod signals if they are inaccurate or abused.

Submit Canonical URLs Only: Always place clean, canonical versions of URLs inside your sitemap file rather than parameter-tagged tracking URLs to help guide Google’s canonical selection.

"Couldn't Fetch" Isn't Always a Syntax Error: If Search Console reports "Couldn't fetch" on a valid, accessible XML file, the cause is often host load throttling or low crawl demand linked to perceived site quality.

(Credit: Google)

How to read the Indexing Report

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

Chapters 0:00 - Introduction: Should we all be using Markdown?
3:45 - The history and purpose of Markdown.
7:15 - Why developers love it: Separation of style and content.
11:20 - Do crawlers need Markdown to understand your site?
14:50 - The danger of "parallel versions" and dynamic rendering lessons.
17:30 - Discussing the "llms.txt" proposal and AI agents. 21:00 - Where Markdown actually makes sense (Developer Docs).
24:00 - Final verdict: Stick to HTML for the web.

Microsoft just offered a Voluntary Exit to around 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada and India. Indian employees have until December 1 to decide.

Nobody has been fired yet. But here's what most people are missing.

In India, a severance package is taxed just like salary, at your slab rate.

The only relief is ₹5 lakh, and only through two routes:

Retrenchment compensation, which applies only when the company removes you and only to non supervisory staff. A voluntary exit doesn't qualify.

VRS, which applies only if the scheme meets strict government conditions like 10 years of service or age 40. Many younger employees won't qualify.

So on a ₹20 lakh severance package, over ₹6 lakh can go straight to tax.

You lose your job, then pay tax on the money meant to carry you to the next one.

And that ₹5 lakh limit has stayed frozen for over two decades, while the gratuity limit has risen to ₹20 lakh.

With tech companies cutting jobs to fund AI, more Indians will face this every year.

Severance is survival money, not a bonus. It's time to make it tax free, or at least raise the limit sharply.

Should severance be taxed in India? 👇

Should you publish your content as a PDF or stick strictly to standard HTML?

Does Google treat PDF files differently when it comes to indexing, ranking, and AI search features?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team demystify how Google Search handles PDF documents.

They break down some of Google's internal pipelines, explain why putting an LLMs.txt file inside a PDF is a bad idea, explore common technical traps like rasterized pages and canonicalization issues, and share practical advice on managing PDFs for SEO, AEO (SEO), and user experience.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   Google's PDF converter pipeline: How Google converts binary PDF containers into HTML pages during indexing so the rest of the pipeline can process them normally.

LLMs.txt as a PDF: Why saving an LLMs.txt file as a PDF is a bad idea, even if you like LLMs.txt.     File limits & Project Gutenberg: Why crawling limits exist, and how HTML and PDF size limits function in the crawl pipeline.

Rasterized pages & accessibility: How pages saved as images destroy text readability, ruin screen reader accessibility, and prevent Google from extracting text content.

Canonicalization & "binary blobs": Why identical PDF downloads across different sites make canonicalization harder and how using rel="canonical" HTTP headers or embedded header links can help.

PDFs for SEO in AI Overviews: How PDFs are parsed, ranked, and referenced in Google Search, AI Overviews, and broader AI systems for training and grounding.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

HTML is preferred, and PDFs work: HTML offers better mobile responsiveness, zoom reflow, and faster loading.

Internally, Google converts indexable PDF text into HTML so they can rank normally and appear in AI features.

Test for text indexability: Highlight and copy text out of your PDF into a text editor; if text doesn't copy, it might be a rasterized image and can't be indexed easily.

For restaurant menus: A PDF menu is better than no menu at all for restaurants, but a responsive HTML web page provides superior performance, accessibility, and user experience. (Credit: Google)

Do sitemaps still matter?
https://t.co/Gdz66VVykn

1 October 2026

Sitemaps have been a core element of web development and search engine optimization for two decades, yet Search Console warnings like "Couldn't fetch" continue to generate concern among site owners.

Are XML sitemaps still necessary with modern search crawlers, or can search engines and AI bots figure out site structure on their own?

In this episode of Search off the Record, Google Search Relations team members Martin Splitt and John Mueller break down the history, technical specifications, and some misconceptions surrounding sitemaps, RSS feeds, LLMs.txt, canonicalization signals, and Search Console indexing behaviors.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Origins of Sitemaps: How early web crawling challenges led to the sitemap standard and how building a sitemap generator started John Mueller's career at Google.

Obsolete vs. Active XML Fields: Why Google dropped support for the priority and changefreq tags, and how the lastmod date is actually evaluated.

XML Sitemaps vs. RSS Feeds: How RSS feeds function as lightweight sitemaps for recent updates and why AI training crawlers utilize both.     Technical Limits & Index Files: The exact URL (50,000) and file size (50MB uncompressed) limits, alongside best practices for sitemap index files and robots.txt declarations.

HTML Sitemaps & LLMs.txt: Why user-facing HTML maps and Markdown-based LLMs.txt files cannot replace structured XML sitemaps for search engines.     Troubleshooting "Couldn't Fetch": How host load management and perceived site quality (crawl demand) trigger non-technical fetching errors in Search Console.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

Keep Sitemaps Enabled by Default: Even for small websites or dynamic CMS setups, keeping auto-generated sitemaps active carries no downside and assists with discovery as sites grow.

Provide Accurate lastmod Timestamps: Avoid setting all page timestamps to the current date; Google evaluates date reliability and will ignore lastmod signals if they are inaccurate or abused.

Submit Canonical URLs Only: Always place clean, canonical versions of URLs inside your sitemap file rather than parameter-tagged tracking URLs to help guide Google’s canonical selection.

"Couldn't Fetch" Isn't Always a Syntax Error: If Search Console reports "Couldn't fetch" on a valid, accessible XML file, the cause is often host load throttling or low crawl demand linked to perceived site quality.

(Credit: Google)

How to read the Indexing Report

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

Do sitemaps still matter?
https://t.co/1NBbsypmox

1 October 2026

Sitemaps have been a core element of web development and search engine optimization for two decades, yet Search Console warnings like "Couldn't fetch" continue to generate concern among site owners.

Are XML sitemaps still necessary with modern search crawlers, or can search engines and AI bots figure out site structure on their own?

In this episode of Search off the Record, Google Search Relations team members Martin Splitt and John Mueller break down the history, technical specifications, and some misconceptions surrounding sitemaps, RSS feeds, LLMs.txt, canonicalization signals, and Search Console indexing behaviors.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Origins of Sitemaps: How early web crawling challenges led to the sitemap standard and how building a sitemap generator started John Mueller's career at Google.

Obsolete vs. Active XML Fields: Why Google dropped support for the priority and changefreq tags, and how the lastmod date is actually evaluated.

XML Sitemaps vs. RSS Feeds: How RSS feeds function as lightweight sitemaps for recent updates and why AI training crawlers utilize both.     Technical Limits & Index Files: The exact URL (50,000) and file size (50MB uncompressed) limits, alongside best practices for sitemap index files and robots.txt declarations.

HTML Sitemaps & LLMs.txt: Why user-facing HTML maps and Markdown-based LLMs.txt files cannot replace structured XML sitemaps for search engines.     Troubleshooting "Couldn't Fetch": How host load management and perceived site quality (crawl demand) trigger non-technical fetching errors in Search Console.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

Keep Sitemaps Enabled by Default: Even for small websites or dynamic CMS setups, keeping auto-generated sitemaps active carries no downside and assists with discovery as sites grow.

Provide Accurate lastmod Timestamps: Avoid setting all page timestamps to the current date; Google evaluates date reliability and will ignore lastmod signals if they are inaccurate or abused.

Submit Canonical URLs Only: Always place clean, canonical versions of URLs inside your sitemap file rather than parameter-tagged tracking URLs to help guide Google’s canonical selection.

"Couldn't Fetch" Isn't Always a Syntax Error: If Search Console reports "Couldn't fetch" on a valid, accessible XML file, the cause is often host load throttling or low crawl demand linked to perceived site quality.

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

text:
How other countries would compete
Governments would bid with tax abatements, land grants, infrastructure, subsidies, streamlined permits, and market access. Likely contenders include:
•  Mexico: Already discussed for a Tesla Gigafactory (Nuevo León has offered substantial incentives). Nearshoring benefits under USMCA, lower costs, and proximity make it attractive for EV assembly and suppliers.
•  China: Existing high-volume Shanghai Gigafactory. Strong manufacturing ecosystem, large domestic market, and historical incentives. Highest geopolitical and IP risk for sensitive tech.
•  Germany / EU: Existing Berlin factory with expansion plans. Talent, regulatory alignment for European markets, and green industrial policy. Higher labor and energy costs.
•  India: Actively courting EV manufacturing with incentive schemes and a large potential market. Cost advantages; Tesla has explored entry.
•  Gulf states (UAE, Saudi Arabia): Capital, energy resources, and aggressive tech-hub incentives. Possible for AI, energy, or non-sensitive manufacturing.
•  Canada: Proximity, talent, and existing battery-equipment ties.
•  Others (Indonesia for battery minerals, Morocco as an emerging EV export base) could compete for specific pieces.
Competition would be fiercest for Tesla’s vehicle and energy manufacturing. SpaceX pieces (especially anything ITAR-controlled or under DoD contracts) would face far higher barriers and limited foreign interest or eligibility.

text:
Daily Digest-10/28

📷S&P 500 NASDAQ DOW RUSSELL 2000

US stocks closed modestly higher for a third session as Fed held rates and signaled data dependence while after-hours tech earnings moved Nasdaq futures lower

The S&P 500 ($SPX) rose 0.28% to 7,743.98, the Dow Jones ($DJI) gained 0.19% to 52,475.10, the Nasdaq Composite ($COMP) advanced 0.27% to 26,549.85, and the Russell 2000 (IWM) climbed 0.41% to 2,830.51.

The Federal Reserve under Chair Kevin Warsh kept its target range at 3.75%-4.00% and signaled data dependence into the December meeting, with Governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a 25-basis-point hike.
Eight of 11 S&P 500 sectors finished higher, led by technology and energy, while utilities and real estate lagged.
Oracle (ORCL) jumped about 11% after its investor day projected at least $225 billion in fiscal 2030 revenue, roughly $30 billion in positive free cash flow by fiscal 2029, and peaking AI capital spending.
Vertiv Holdings (VRT) climbed 16.5% after reporting earnings that beat estimates and highlighting bullish long-term AI infrastructure demand.
Semiconductor stocks outperformed, with Micron Technology (MU) gaining about 5.9% and Broadcom (AVGO) adding roughly 2.8%.
Wendy’s (WEN) advanced after a Nelson Peltz–led Trian Fund Management group offered about $1.4 billion to take the company private.
F5 Inc. (FFIV) fell more than 20% after beating fiscal fourth-quarter estimates as fiscal 2027 guidance for 8–9% revenue growth and warnings of second-half deceleration and near-term margin pressure disappointed, while Lumentum (LITE) gained on news of a possible sale to Marvell Technology (MRVL).
In after-hours trading, Microsoft (MSFT) climbed about 2% after fiscal Q1 revenue of $92.28 billion and adjusted EPS of $4.89 beat estimates, driven by 48% Azure growth as Azure revenue reached $33.2 billion, while Alphabet (GOOGL) dropped sharply after Q3 revenue of $127.6 billion and EPS of $2.12 missed expectations amid weaker ad sales and negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, and ServiceNow (NOW) slid after issuing fourth-quarter revenue guidance below estimates.
Nasdaq 100 futures (@NQ) fell nearly 1% after the bell even as T-Mobile (TMUS), KLA (KLAC), and Equinix (EQIX) beat estimates, with investors looking ahead to key economic data due on October 29.

text:
Grok Bot just got an update with v0.78.1! 🚀

Shopping cards and subscription templates
Also includes v0.78.0

Changelog v0.78.1

New:
• Shopping with a Bot shows products as cards with photos, rating, price, and store, plus up to two badges such as Top rated.
• Three or four product results scroll in a carousel, and you can swipe through each product's photos.
• On a product page, in-stock options come first, options no store has are disabled, and Buy now starts an order you approve.
• After you place an order, the Bot tracks it and tells you when it ships or arrives, and shipment cards show the carrier and stage.
• Connect Shop Pay in the Vault's Payments tab, then pick it in Pay with or make it the payment method Bots use first.
• The Try it, don't pay for it template starts a free trial for you and cancels it, or reminds you, before it bills.
• The Find unused subscriptions template cancels plans you pick from the ones you still pay for, and Watch subscription prices checks renewal prices.
• Bots can cancel a subscription or look up its price and renewal date, and confirm with you before changing anything.
• On an Apple silicon Mac, the Intel version of Grok Bot offers to download the Apple silicon version.
• Editing a Vault contact offers Add email, Add phone, and Make primary.
• Bots can start cloud agents in a custom mode you name, and keep replying to them in it.
• In Share, Who has access lists your team and organization, and a Team Bot can be limited to Only you. (Teams)
• Managers can add logins to a Team Bot's own Vault in Configure, under Tools, and the Bot signs in with them for the team. (Teams)

Improved:
• App cards, plugin rows, sign-in errors, and connector errors the Bot relays show the connector's name instead of an internal ID.
• The Bot's browser types one character at a time and moves the mouse on every website it fills in.
• On Cloudflare, Coinbase, Gusto, YouTube, Railway, Google Ads, Meta Ads, and TikTok for Business sign-in pages, the Bot offers that connector.
• In Slack, people whose account isn't linked learn that some features are limited and how to link it, including in threads the Bot follows.
• Where Grok Bot offered a free trial, it now offers Get Grok Bot with a unified plan and See Unified Plans.
• When a connector needs a permission its connection can't request, the Bot says reconnecting won't help.
• When you set up Grok Bot from X, the first reply no longer waits for all of your X data to load.
• Asking what a Bot can connect to leads with up to three apps to connect.
• Bots apply several Page edits at once, and leave the Page unchanged if any edit doesn't fit.
• Secure Forms that only ask for a sign-in code arrive without an extra explanation.
• Computer settings name the Bots that updating the computer would stop.
• Approval and draft cards no longer name the older Allow rule removed to make room on a full list.
• Connect apps lists apps you connected through Grok under From Grok, and every Connect button there has the same width.
• The Vault toolbar stays on one row with a More menu, and Vault settings use the same card style as other settings.
• Share in a Page header matches the Share button on Team Bots, and the share dialog's intro wraps more evenly.
• Attachments staged in the message box are more compact.
• In the full-screen viewer, captions sit closer to the image.
• The Add skills dialog no longer shows a Back button on its library step.
• The Get Grok Bot for mobile menu item is shorter in Portuguese.
• Usage breakdowns from a Bot label the catch-all row Deleted bots, group chats and other people's bots.
• When your team limits sharing, share controls say Only team admins can share Bots. (Teams)
• A team Page appears in the Library under every Bot that published it. (Teams)
• Team Bot Library rows show a Pin button on hover, and a pinned row keeps its pin visible. (Teams)
• When a Team Bot routine needs one of your connectors, it asks in the routine's Slack thread and tags you. (Teams)
• On the team dashboard, Bot computers groups setup scripts, setup files, and team secrets, and one Security & compliance card holds computer controls. (Teams)
• The team dashboard's Status card has Download and Copy link for the desktop app. (Teams)
• The Grok Bot admin page says Shared Bots, with Manage Shared Bots and Create Bot. (Teams)

Fixed:
• Copy on a reply keeps headings, lists, and links when you paste into Slack, Gmail, Docs, or Notion, and copied selections paste as markdown.
• Scrolling a long chat after you resize the window no longer jumps.
• Specific working statuses show right away, while generic ones like Working on it and Thinking wait a moment first.
• For a greeting, thanks, or small talk, the working status says "is on it" or "is working on it".
• Update installs the version you clicked, and an open Update ready dialog switches to the newest finished download.
• Update stays on Restarting… until the restart begins, and when a restart is refused, every Update button says why.
• Single-choice question cards show Something else again, so you can type your own answer.
• In question cards, Enter no longer sends your typed answer while an input method is still composing text.
• The Bot's computer card stays on Asleep during brief background wakes and shows Waking up… as soon as you wake it.
• A Bot can take back a reaction it added to your message, and the reaction comes off in the chat.
• Task lists and thread names refresh after the app reconnects instead of staying stale.
• Switching accounts no longer lets a late reply from the previous account change or pin the new account's main Bot.
• Clicking the current Bot in the sidebar closes an open Page.
• The Drop files to add to chat overlay no longer gets stuck when a Page opens or closes during a drag.
• Diagrams on a Page wrap long labels instead of clipping them, and lines meet each node at its own point.
• A pull request chip whose status can't load stays plain in the sentence, and its hover card offers Try again.
• The usage limit banner closes once you're back under your limit.
• Back from a connector returns to the screen you came from and keeps your Vault tab.
• After 10 minutes, a connect card asks Still signing in? instead of saying the sign-in didn't finish.
• When a connector is briefly busy signing in, its connect card and Slack sign-in link still appear.
• A connector sign-in that needs setup first says what to add and opens the plugin page.
• Signing in to a Google account that's already connected reuses it, with one reconnect card instead of several.
• Google Calendar asks you to reconnect only when signing in again can grant the missing permission.
• Connector tools stay listed when a connector changes while its tool list is loading.
• When a plugin isn't available, the Bot says so instead of listing the whole catalog.
• Connect cards for Railway, Square, TradingView, and Google Ads appear only on those services' own pages.
• Gmail drafts the Bot writes in plain text open in rich text, so they read well on a phone and send without hard line breaks.
• Gmail drafts and sends can attach a file from the Bot's computer in more cases.
• Bot emails retry once when the mail server connection times out.
• A Slack connect link opened while signed in to another account works once you sign in as the right account and connect again.
• Remove from Slack now disconnects Slack.
• With Route traffic through this computer on, Settings says when Grok Bot's computer is asleep and that routing reconnects when it wakes.
• With Route traffic through this computer on, pages no longer fail right away when only another host on them is refused.
• Approved browser actions no longer fail on some Bot computers when the page hasn't changed.
• The computer view follows the browser tab the Bot brings to the front.
• Saving a file from the Bot's computer shows Couldn't save this file if the file changes during the download.
• Files already saved in another chat, such as Slack uploads to a Team Bot, save in the new chat instead of failing.
• When the Bot's computer has been refusing saves, Reset and Recover keep the current disk instead of restoring an older backup.
• Grok Bot starts your computer while your accounts are being merged.
• Routines made in a new Bot's first chat run in your time zone instead of UTC.
• Two saves to the same memory at once no longer overwrite each other.
• Image creation stops with a clear error when a reference image can't be read, instead of ignoring it.
• Spend totals the Bot records use the right currency, so other currencies aren't counted as US dollars.
• Bots using the built-in code review tools act with your access and never approve your own pull request.
• Order cards leave out Ship to for orders that ship nothing, and orders through a store's connector pay with that connector's own options.
• The Tailscale plugin shows Not available yet on accounts that can't use it, instead of installing a plugin that can't connect.
• In Connect Apps, logos made of a single glyph show whole in their tiles.
• Under General, an account with no name shows Enter your name on the Account card.
• Clicking a webhook routine opens its details, including the webhook URL.
• In Turkish, emoji search matches a typed dotted I.
• Buying a plan during desktop sign-in returns you to the approval screen, so the app finishes signing in.
• Share works for people on more than one team with no team selected. (Teams)
• A Team Bot's Shared with your team list shows only Pages that Bot made. (Teams)
• Shared with you includes a large team's most-used Bots when the list is too long to show every Bot. (Teams)
• The Team Bots list loads when one access check times out instead of failing. (Teams)
• People on several teams with none selected can publish a public Bot template when their teams allow it. (Teams)
• Team Bots search Slack when asked instead of refusing after a note that other sessions can't be opened. (Teams)
• Team Bots explain correctly where a teammate's Slack channel listener reports. (Teams)
• A Team Bot tells managers they can change its name and picture from their own chat with it. (Teams)
• With Terminate Inactive Computers on, a computer counts as inactive after 30 days without a message to any of its Bots. (Enterprise)

text:
Grok Bot just got an update with v0.77.0! 🚀

Permissions, Vault payments, and question cards
Also includes v0.76.0

Changelog v0.77.0

New:
• 1Password connects without a shared vault: you approve each login in 1Password, which fills it in the Bot's browser without the Bot seeing it. Requires Grok Bot 0.68.0 or later.
• Import Memory to Grok Bot, in Settings, brings your preferences and context from another AI assistant into your primary Bot. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• Bots can ask several questions on one card that steps through them, with Your own answer when none of the choices fit.
• Tables in chat have a copy button that copies them for Slack or as markdown, and wide tables open full screen with zoom.
• The Vault has a Payments tab where you pick the payment method Bots use first, and you still approve every purchase.
• Address fields in forms and the Vault suggest streets as you type, and a ZIP code fills in the city and state.
• When Gmail signs you out, such as after Google revokes access, your primary Bot tells you in its chat and offers to reconnect.
• After you connect your first app, the Bot offers one more that pairs with it, such as Google Calendar after Gmail.
• Português (Portugal) joins the app's languages, and Brazilian Portuguese is now labeled Português (Brasil).
• Right-click an emoji to pin it, and pinned emoji lead your quick reactions.
• Page owners can delete a Page from the Library, which removes it for everyone it was shared with.
• Order Concierge and Deal Watcher templates track your orders, refunds, and returns, and watch prices and coupons, never buying without your OK.
• Bots can update a saved Vault entry's name, hint, and card details for you.
• Custom MCP servers that use a private certificate authority work once you approve that authority.
• In a DM with a Team Bot, teammates can have it message other Team Bots they can use. (Teams)
• In Slack, Team Bots can edit messages they posted and remove reactions they added. (Teams)
• Team admins can limit Bot sharing to admins, and share controls then say Your admin has disabled Bot sharing. (Teams)
• Enterprise audit logs record changes to a team's trusted CA certificates. (Enterprise)

Improved:
• Grok Bot has a new typeface for text and code, including on Pages. Requires Grok Bot 0.68.0 or later.
• A Bot's working status is a short phrase in your language, in the app and in Slack.
• Connector buttons say Connect everywhere, a signed-out connector shows Not connected, and Your plugins offers Reconnect for one that stopped working. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• In Connect Apps, Add installs a plugin and opens its sign-in in one click, and Add and Uninstall finish as soon as they're saved. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• Plugins show Connecting… while you sign in and Connected once you're done.
• Auto-review lets through more private actions you can undo without an approval card, and keeps an approval when only your open tabs change.
• Background work you start in your own words no longer asks for Auto-review approval to start.
• Auto-review approval cards stay open for 30 minutes instead of 10, in the app and in Slack.
• Settings has a Permissions section that lists Auto-review rules under Always Ask and Allow without Asking, each with its own Add Rule button. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• Auto-review rule cards in chat show each rule as a sentence and name any older Allow rule removed to make room.
• Approval cards name a connector by its service, adding the account when two accounts share a name.
• Dictation writes words into the message box while you're still speaking.
• Email draft cards have a Discard button again, so you can drop a draft without sending it.
• Section headings in Settings, such as Appearance, now have Copy link too, not just individual settings.
• The command palette shows each Bot's latest message and link text instead of markdown, and on a Mac moves with Ctrl-N and Ctrl-P.
• The dock badge counts unread conversations instead of unread messages.
• Wide tables show scroll arrows when you hover over them.
• Vault entries have a Hints field that tells Bots when to use each one.
• Saved addresses, phones, and emails appear together as Contact info in the Vault, and one contact can hold several emails and phone numbers.
• Bots try your saved Vault logins and cards before a password manager or another way to pay.
• The Vault lists the Bot's own email first, and editing a saved login shows the password masked, with Remove on the form.
• When an app you ask for isn't installed, the Bot checks the plugin catalog and links the app's page in Connect Apps.
• When the Bot hands you its computer to sign in to sites like Google, GitHub, or QuickBooks, it offers their connector, and connecting ends the handoff.
• When an app connects without a sign-in, the Bot carries on with your task in the same reply.
• The Bot removes or renames a connector only when you name that change yourself.
• A plugin's accounts row says when a sign-in is waiting or didn't finish.
• When you name an app in Chinese, Japanese, or Korean, plugin search finds it by those words or retries with its English name.
• Slack message drafts show a formatted preview and who the message notifies, and warn you when Slack can't confirm the channel.
• In Slack, the Bot checks what a reply is answering before acting, and in DMs it answers follow-ups in their thread.
• In shared Slack conversations, the Bot checks each post against who can read it before sending.
• Someone who DMs a Bot in Slack without a linked account gets one Connect Slack account notice.
• When a safety filter stops a computer task, the Bot tries again on another model before asking you to do that step.
• Browser screenshots the Bot saves keep their full size, including tall pages, instead of a smaller copy.
• Keys that apps on the Bot's computer store in the system keyring, such as Okta Verify's, now survive when the computer is recreated.
• The Bot pays in a set order instead of asking which wallet to use, and offers Link one-time cards only in the US and Canada.
• Asked what happens if an order goes wrong, the Bot cites only protections it has read and doesn't promise refunds.
• When X Money isn't set up on your X account, the Bot links the Money tab on X.
• When you ask a Bot to schedule something and no calendar is connected, it offers Google Calendar first, or Outlook Calendar if you use Outlook.
• When your plan doesn't include routines, the Bot names the plan that does.
• Every email a Bot sends from its own address to one other person now includes a one-click unsubscribe, not just the first.
• Bots no longer send email to addresses that have permanently bounced.
• Follow-ups to a running cloud agent the Bot started reach it right away.
• Pictures on a Page fade in, and broken ones show their description.
• File icons in chat and the Library have a new design.
• Opening or closing the details pane slides the chat along with it.
• Dialogs share consistent widths, and Connect Apps and the keyboard shortcuts sheet are wider.
• With several apps connected, the sidebar footer folds Connect apps into an icon beside your name and no longer flashes open at launch.
• Settings shows a single banner for combining your subscriptions into one plan.
• Plugins a team admin wouldn't allow show Disabled by team admin. (Teams)
• Team admins choose whether members can publish Bot templates publicly, only to the team, or not at all. (Teams)

Fixed:
• 1Password fills recover from more problems, such as a sleeping extension or an expired approval, and the Bot continues as soon as you approve.
• On Windows and Linux, the Bot notices an installed 1Password app and can offer to connect it.
• A message the server already accepted stays delivered, and Resend on one marked Not delivered yet sends it.
• The chat stays steady while you scroll past tables and links or after zooming, and dragging a selection past a wide table scrolls it.
• Desktop notifications close once you read the reply or the Bot stops waiting, and use the Bot's current name.
• Answered questions stay answered, and unread counts no longer jump back.
• Opening a chat shows its messages even when marking it read fails.
• Images you send no longer flash gray after uploading, and camera photos keep their upright size.
• In a long chat, two messages sent a moment apart both get answers.
• When one of your Bots wakes another to do work, the second Bot's questions come to the chat where you asked.
• Saved logins and cards fill more reliably, including on subdomains and Shopify checkouts, and stay out of unrelated fields.
• Importing passwords from a CSV file skips each login's notes so long ones don't block it, and a full Vault says how many didn't fit.
• Background work stops calling a connector that signed you out and tells you to reconnect it.
• Connect cards appear only when a connector says you need to sign in, not for other errors.
• Connect cards keep waiting while your newest sign-in page is open, and a refused sign-in sends you back to Grok Bot with the reason.
• Connector sign-ins can finish up to an hour after you start them.
• When Google throttles requests, Google apps stay connected and the Bot says to try again later instead of asking you to reconnect.
• A Google account without Gmail stays connected, and the Bot asks for an account that has Gmail.
• Adding a second Gmail or Google Drive account opens Google's account picker, and removing one account leaves the others in place.
• Gmail replies quote the original so Gmail folds the thread, signature logos stay inline, and failed Gmail reads and sends retry.
• Ask first and Block rules for Gmail searches and reads hold even when the Bot calls them by another name.
• Signing in from a connect card resumes the Bot for more apps, such as QuickBooks, Zoho, and Workday, and for teammates on a Team Bot.
• Jira and Confluence requests find your site on the first try.
• Vercel runtime log requests that reach past your plan's retention return the logs it keeps.
• A connector whose server refuses registration shows Error instead of a sign-in that can't work.
• A connector access card that expires or is interrupted says so, and the Bot knows the action didn't run.
• When background work needs one of your apps, the Bot asks with an allow card in the app, or Allow once and Skip in Slack.
• In Slack, people without a linked Grok Bot account can't use the owner's logins or private data through the owner's Bot.
• In Slack, a Bot can still read its thread and channels when a Slack connector is also connected or connector lookup fails.
• In Slack, a message the Bot sends without naming a conversation posts once, in the current conversation.
• After a failed Slack turn, a retry reads the whole thread.
• Slack routines that listen for messages see images on the message that started them.
• Settings and sidebar changes that can't be saved go back to the saved state, and folder changes from two devices no longer overwrite each other.
• When usage can't load, Usage & Billing keeps the last reading with Try again, even after a relaunch.
• When an update is ready while a Bot is working, Grok Bot offers Stop and Update.
• A Bot's template skills show under Private skills, labeled From template.
• Links to Grok Bot inside a Page open in the app, and a Page opened from the Library shows a save made while it loaded.
• After you're removed from a team, your personal Pages show in the Library again.
• Teammates see Pages shared with the team in a Team Bot's Library, under Shared with your team. (Teams)
• Mentions of Bots with names longer than one word open that Bot.
• Names, titles, and instructions cut at a length limit no longer split an emoji.
• The full-screen media viewer's title follows the item on screen.
• The computer view leaves Waking up once the screen is ready.
• Taking over the Bot's computer to sign in with a security key opens the security key prompt.
• The Bot's computer stays up when memory runs low and recovers faster after a crash, so fewer turns end on Couldn't Reach Grok Bot's Computer.
• Commands on the Bot's computer that wait for input, such as package install prompts, finish instead of hanging.
• The Bot's browser keeps site logins after its last window closes, and Apple ID sign-in forms fill correctly.
• With Route traffic through this computer on, plain http pages load, and the Bot says when your computer goes offline.
• Commands a Bot runs on your computer keep going while a file copies to it.
• Commits a cloud agent makes keep your co-author line.
• Reconnect on X Money starts a fresh sign-in.
• The time zone picker includes Europe/Kyiv.
• In right-to-left languages, full-screen viewer close buttons sit clear of the window controls.
• White connector logos stay visible in the light theme.
• After an account merge, an account with no Bots sees Meet Grok Bot.
• Going Back from a plugin whose sign-in you didn't finish shows Connect again instead of Reconnect. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• The Cumulative Spend chart scales to the spend it shows. (Enterprise)
• Linked teammates on a Team Bot use their own connectors and memory. (Teams)
• A Team Bot that acknowledges a request without answering follows up with the answer. (Teams)
• A published Team Bot no longer says everyone on the team can use it. (Teams)
• Share on a Team Bot's team access card gives the team access. (Teams)
• In a teammate's 1:1 with a Team Bot, notes about them saved in another chat carry over. (Teams)
• In a teammate's own chat with your Team Bot, computer permission buttons are disabled. (Teams)
• On a Team Bot, a teammate whose app account has a label can sign in from the connect card. (Teams)
• Team Bots follow the skill guide of a connector a teammate allowed. (Teams)

text:
Grok Bot just got an update with v0.75.8! 🚀

Auto-review rule cards and smarter connectors
Also includes v0.75.6 and v0.75.7

Changelog v0.75.8

New:
• In the app, a Bot can offer to add, change, or remove one of your Auto-review rules on a card you confirm. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.

Improved:
• Auto-review takes a second look before showing an approval card, so fewer safe actions need one.
• A Bot's status line shows up right after you send, even for quick replies.
• When background work finishes, the Bot completes what you asked, including steps you said to take once it was done, and says what it would do next instead of acting on its own or on another agent's approval. Requires Grok Bot 0.75.2 or later.
• Auto-review no longer counts a Bot saving or editing one of its routines as risky by itself.
• Auto-review approval cards in Slack describe the action, as they do in the app.
• Scheduling uses the calendar you've connected, Google Calendar or Outlook Calendar, and offers to connect one only when neither is.
• In a chat only you can see, a Bot reads your own private files without asking first.
• When a Bot installs a plugin while working, it can use the plugin's skills right away.
• People not on a Team Bot's share list, including teammates, no longer have access to it until an owner shares it with them. (Teams)

Fixed:
• When a connector such as X adds tools or fields, Bots can use them without you reconnecting it.
• A connector whose sign-in expired shows Authenticate in the app instead of Connected, matching what the Bot says. Requires Grok Bot 0.71.2 or later.
• Images a connector returns as files reach the Bot as images, and other binary files are no longer read as garbled text.
• X Money connects in one tap for more X accounts, and if it can't connect yours, the Bot says so instead of offering a sign-in.
• When a Bot posts to Slack for you, such as from a routine, your phone isn't notified and its unread badge doesn't go up.
• In Slack, when a safety check blocks a Bot's reply, the Bot says so and suggests trying a different message.
• For most accounts, with Route traffic through this computer on, the connection comes back as soon as the Bot's computer wakes.
• A Team Bot's routines can read Slack channels you and the Bot are both in, instead of refusing every read. (Teams)
• When a Team Bot edits one of its own Slack messages, the message shows a muted (edited) label. (Teams)

THE GREAT COSMIC LIQUIDATION OF PLANET EARTH
Or how we became trillionaires and still can’t afford bread

OPERATION BLACKOUT #1 & 2 

The most expensive raid on your nap

I. CONGRATULATIONS! WE WON!
According to the announcement nobody can verify

Friends, ladies and gentlemen, and all the other confused species that pay taxes:

Excellent news! Last night, while you were snoring and varnishing your pillow with saliva, an ultra-secret military superintelligence commando unit launched OPERATION BLACKOUT #1

These are the geniuses who hack the universe before coffee but announce their secret operations on YouTube. With mattress ads!

The target? According to the story: the Deep State, the Cabal, “the Zionists,” the global financial system, and the international operating system of darkness. The entire apocalypse enemy catalog, now on sale!

BOOM! Massive attack. No mercy. No receipt

The result? TOTAL VICTORY! We control the “universal logarithm of the entire existing system.

Yes: LOGARITHM. Not algorithm. Because when you don’t understand math, you change a few letters and get promoted to quantum commander

II. THE MIRACULOUS HANDOUT
Millionaires in theory, in dreams, and in Narnia

All the confiscated money will be distributed among EVERY inhabitant of planet Earth. Exclusively. Martians are out because they don’t have proof of address

Money from drugs, thousands of fraudulent operations, banks, politicians, reptilians, the Illuminati, and all the cartels

Applause! Confetti! Make the lizard pay

Every child in Africa, every grandpa in Farmingdale, every influencer crying on TikTok: ALL MILLIONAIRES!

It’s communism on steroids with Wi-Fi. Universal redistribution with drones and a podcast!

Imagine eight billion people checking their balances simultaneously. The system crashes. The ATM explodes. The bank sends

“Congratulations: you have 47 trillion dollars.”

We’re rich! We’re free! We’re customers on hold!

III. THE FINE PRINT OF THE APOCALYPSE
Your fortune comes with a padlock

But there’s a condition. Always. Like marriage or those terms we accept without reading, signing away custody of our pancreas

Those fortunes:
You can’t sell them.
You can’t redeem them.
You can’t spend them.

Excuse me WHAT THE FUCK?

They gave me all the money in the world, but I can’t use it!

It’s like giving you a Ferrari with no engine, wheels, or doors, inside a display case, in another country. And you’re dead. But what an elegant estate!

Before, you were poor with twenty dollars. Now you’re poor with twenty TRILLION in an account that won’t open. Progress!

An abstract millionaire. Conceptual. Philosophically solvent. Spiritually rolling in cash that somebody else holds for you

IV. A METAPHOR FOR USEFUL IDIOTS
The coupon even its creator won’t accept

They handed us the biggest coupon in the universe. We went to redeem it:

“Oh, no. It was a metaphor.”
“Perfect. Do they accept metaphors at the bakery?”
“No. But you can smell the bread and visualize abundance

V. SLEEP TIGHT
We’ll be the richest people in the cemetery

The superintelligence “controls everything.” “There are no more bad guys, financial systems, or darkness.

Just us, sitting on a mountain of imaginary gold, explaining to the kids:

“We’re trillionaires.
“What’s for dinner?”
“White rice again. The wealth is undergoing maintenance

Free from the terrible burden of spending money

Welcome to the future: everybody owns everything and we have nothing

OPERATION BLACKOUT #2
The end of the world: bring your own sandwich

And here comes the next announcement: “Prepare water, food, and some cash for a few days

Of course! Money is disappearing, but bring exact change

They promise the end of the enslaving financial system and its replacement with the QFS. “Don’t worry about anything or anyone

Peace of mind is included; evidence is pending

text:
Little Richard sold the publishing rights to "Tutti Frutti" for $50. His record deal paid him half a cent per record. In 1988 he walked onto the Grammy stage to present an award and announced the winner was him: "I have never received nothing!"

The clip opens on that moment. Then Little Richard on Letterman, explaining where the money went. Listen to the line about counting.

He went from singing on doorsteps in Macon, Georgia, for dimes, to selling out shows around the world. "I was making $15 a week, and all of a sudden I'm making $10,000 an hour." He went back to school to learn to count and read, because he didn't know how to handle the money. "I had a lot of managers. Taking it all, leaving me nothing."

The error bar on his money.
His own numbers, on Letterman: $10,000 an hour.
His own numbers, decades later on local TV: "$35,000 a night… then $100,000 an hour."
What he sued his old label for in 1984: $112 million or $115 million, depending on the report. The case was thrown out, then settled years later for an undisclosed sum.
What he settled for in 1959, giving up his royalties on those records: $11,000.
Publishing rights to "Tutti Frutti": $50.
His royalty: half a cent per record.
The big numbers in his story move by 10x depending on who's talking. The only exact numbers are the small ones.

Letterman asked if the songs had made him a wealthy man. "Well, it should have." His managers, he said, were very rich. "I made a lot of money. But I was cheated, I was used, I was exploited."

You're 23, you just wrote the song that will start rock and roll, and the label offers $50 for the publishing today. Nobody can tell you what it's worth. Do you sign?

text:
Oregon Cares: Make preschool affordable for more families
Preschool tuition is a real family expense. Oregon's Preschool Promise offers free preschool to eligible 3- and 4-year-olds, generally up to 200% of the poverty level. A state investment in an earlier start.

The problem. Preschool costs can put early learning out of reach for families with limited income.

What changed. Oregon created Preschool Promise through HB 3380 in 2015. The state-funded program offers free preschool for eligible children ages three and four, generally in households at or below 200% of the federal poverty level.

Why it helps. Participating families avoid preschool tuition while choosing among available school, community and licensed childcare settings. It is a concrete benefit for both children's early learning and household budgets.

Scope. Eligibility does not guarantee an immediate available place. Local capacity, schedules and enrollment rules matter; this is not universal free childcare.

Takeaway. A child's opportunity to start learning should not depend only on a parent's budget.

Action and credit. Governor Brown and Democratic-led legislature; bipartisan program origins

text:
gRialo 🐴 Hello… it's me again 🌿

last time, I was thinking about how nice it would be if an app could still help me after I'd already finished something. I book my Italian restaurant, get my confirmation, and go about my day. then the restaurant suddenly closes early, and instead of finding out when I'm standing outside the door, I get a little heads-up. disappointing news, yes. but much better than showing up hungry and confused 😂🍝

but then I started wondering… what if something changes while I'm not even looking at my phone?

✎ the world doesn't wait for me to check my notifications

let's say I'm finally enjoying my little vacation. I've put my phone in my bag, wandered into a cute bookstore, and somehow spent forty minutes looking at notebooks I absolutely do not need 😂📚

meanwhile, the restaurant sends an update. my reservation has been canceled, and there's an option to request a refund.

but I don't see it.

because I'm busy deciding whether I need a notebook with tiny strawberries on the cover. obviously, I do 😂🍓

and by the time I check my phone, maybe an hour has passed.

now, I don't expect the app to make every decision while I'm gone. imagine opening my phone and discovering it booked another restaurant, changed my plans, and ordered me a taxi without asking.

ummm… excuse me? 😂

but I also don't want everything to stop just because I wasn't staring at my screen.

✎ some things can keep moving without me. others should wait for my yes.

and I think that's a really interesting little balance.

maybe the app can receive the cancellation, update my reservation status, and show me the refund information without needing me to do anything.

great! those are just updates.

but if the restaurant offers a different time, or the refund requires choosing between store credit and getting my money back, that's something I'd want to decide myself.

so maybe when I finally check my phone, I see:

“Your reservation was canceled. Your booking status has been updated. A refund option is available, and we've left the next decision to you.”

ohhh. perfect 🌿

the useful little things have already been taken care of, but nothing important was decided behind my back.

and this is another reason Rialo keeps coming to mind.

one of the things I find interesting about Rialo is how real-world events and onchain actions can be connected through things like reactive transactions and in-protocol APIs.

developers can imagine applications that respond when certain conditions are met, instead of waiting for someone to manually check every update.

and I think that could be especially useful when we're busy doing something else.

maybe a payment status changes while I'm at work. maybe a delivery gets delayed while I'm driving. maybe an event is canceled while I'm having dinner with friends.

I don't want to keep checking everything just in case something happened.

but I also don't want to hand over every decision to an app.

✎ being helpful doesn't mean taking over

and honestly, I think that distinction matters a lot.

because some actions are simple enough to happen in the background. updating a status, recording that something changed, or preparing the information I'll need later.

but other things deserve a little pause.

spending money. accepting a new booking time. changing an important reservation. agreeing to different conditions.

those are the moments when I'd want the app to ask me first.

and with Rialo, I like imagining how developers could build that kind of experience, where automatic responses and user approval work together instead of competing with each other.

of course, the connected services would need to provide reliable information, and the app would need clear rules about what it can and can't do automatically.

but that's what makes the idea interesting to me.

not an app that does absolutely everything for me.

just one that can keep the little things moving while leaving the important choices in my hands.

because I don't want to spend my vacation managing notifications, checking statuses, and wondering whether something changed while I was away.

I want to enjoy my day.

and when I come back to my phone, I'd love to see that the situation is already clear and the next decision is waiting for me.

not ten different problems I have to investigate from the beginning 😂

maybe that's what a really comfortable digital experience would feel like.

the world keeps moving. the information stays connected. the small things can be handled when appropriate, and the big decisions still belong to me.

and honestly, I think that's a pretty lovely balance 🌿

now, if you'll excuse me, I have a very important decision to make.

the strawberry notebook… or the one with the tiny ducks?

actually, I might need both 🐴🌿
